speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As a result of the unavoidable absence of my colleague the Minister of Agriculture, may I on his behalf make a short statement which follows negotiations he and I have had with representatives of the sugar refining company involved and the Ontario government.
The agricultural stabilization board has been authorized to support the price of sugar beets for the year 1961. This will stabilize the returns to sugar beet growers in the sugar beet growing areas, namely in Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and Alberta. Sugar beets for 1961 will be supported on the basis of $13.18, national average price per ton for beets yielding 16 per cent sugar, which is 102 per cent of the 10-year national average price. The prescribed national support price of $13.18 per ton for sugar beets yielding 16 per cent sugar is equivalent to the national average support price in 1960 of $14.23 per ton for sugar beets yielding 17 per cent sugar.
As a result, the support price arrangements for producers in Quebec, Manitoba and Alberta will remain unchanged from last year, and any deficiency payments will be equal to the difference between the prescribed price of $13.18 per ton of sugar beets and the national average price per ton received by producers.
In view of difficulties facing the Ontario sugar beet industry in 1961, a special arrangement, for one year only will apply to sugar beets grown in that province. The Ontario growers have represented to the governments that a return of $13 per ton was
essential to meet their requirements. The processing company has undertaken to raise its purchase price by 50 cents a ton above the original offer. The province of Ontario will make a contribution, equal to 50 cents per ton, toward deficiency payments, payable in that province. Through the co-operation of the company and the province, Ontario growers will be assured of a market at a satisfactory return.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Minister of Finance for this announcement. He will know undoubtedly that several times since the middle of January I have asked the Minister of Agriculture to announce a sugar beet policy for Canada which, he said in the middle of January speaking in Chatham, would be announced within the course of a few days.
Though this announcement comes rather late it is nevertheless very acceptable. When I indicated in the house the other day that in southwestern Ontario seeding operations would begin possibly by the end of March and on that account there ought to be an announcement forthwith, some hon. members did not seem to concur in this statement of fact. But Mr. Bissonet of Stony Point, a well know sugar beet farmer in my riding, said the other day, an announcement of government policy was something that was necessary. The minister recognizes the special situation which attends the Ontario sugar beet farmer, and which puts him in a position somewhat different from that of the sugar beet growers of Quebec and western Canada. Certainly the sugar beet grower in Ontario does not have the transportation freight advantage that exists in the case of the sugar beet grower in western Canada, and that has put him in a difficult position.
It has now been decided that there should be a floor price of $13.18 and the Ontario government is going to assist in the matter somewhat, to the extent of 50 cents a ton. The company has undertaken to make a contribution notwithstanding its alleged loss on its operations with regard to sugar beets in the factory at Chatham, Ontario. I am glad to see the Ontario government providing this assistance. It is emulating the practice of the government of the province of Quebec, a government that has for the past year or so been extending similar assistance.

Order.

Support Price for Sugar Beets

The government's policy of national average prices coupled with deficiency payments has not worked out well for many industries, but to date it seems to have been a reasonably satisfactory policy for the sugar beet industry. At least that is the reaction that has come from the sugar beet growers.
I would have hoped that in announcing this policy the government would have announced a support price, a floor price, rather than a national average price, because very often in practice a national average price does not provide a floor and means lower prices for many producers. However, the sugar beet industry is such that fluctuations in price are not as wide as is the case in other industries. I think this announcement, coupled with the further supplementary guarantees from the government of Ontario and from the sugar beet processors themselves, should work out as a relatively satisfactory policy for one year.
The hon. member for Essex East has said this is not a long term policy. That is correct;

but we are getting a year to year policy from this government, and for the coming year I hope this policy will be extended.

subsubtopic: ELIGIBLE AREAS UNDER DOUBLE DEPRECIATION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make an announcement with respect to the selection of areas eligible for double depreciation under the program announced in the supplementary budget of December 20, 1960.
Hon. members of this house will recall that one objective of this program is to assist new industries in areas where there has been a substantial degree of continued unemployment over the years. Areas which meet the following criteria may qualify under this program. They are broken down into two categories; areas with a labour force of 10,000 and over, and areas with a labour force of less than 10,000. In those areas where the labour force is 10,000 and over the criteria are first, the area must have been classified by the Department of Labour in a surplus labour market category for 75 per cent or more of the 48 summer months from May to October, 19531960. Second, industrial employment must have declined over the period 1953-1960.
Areas with a labour force of less than 10,000 must have been classified by the Department of Labour as in a surplus labour market category for 50 per cent or more of the 48 summer months May to October, 1953-1960. Second, industrial employment conditions must have generally deteriorated over the years.
Areas which qualify will be termed surplus manpower areas. These areas will have the same boundaries as labour market areas served by the national employment service local offices. Localities, as distinct from larger areas, which qualify will be termed surplus manpower localities. These, in most cases, will have the same boundaries as municipalities.
The term "surplus labour market category" used in the criteria, I might explain, has reference to the classification of labour markets which has been published monthly in the Labour Gazette by the Department of Labour since 1953.
Applications may be made by municipal authorities wishing to be considered for designation as a surplus manpower area or locality under this program. Examples of areas and localities which might qualify under this program are Springhill, Elliot
Inquiries of the Ministry Lake and certain localities in Cape Breton. The applications would be made to the Department of Labour, which would undertake the necessary investigations, in cooperation with the national employment service, to determine whether the areas and localities meet the required criteria. Based on the findings of these investigations, the areas and localities which qualified would be designated by the governor in council.

On December 20 the Minister of Finance, in the only reference he made to unemployment, said the government proposed to embark on a program of double depreciation to assist in the relocation of industry and to encourage industry in depressed or chronically underemployed areas. However, no announcement concerning detail has been forthcoming until today.
Much time has been wasted, during which industries and municipalities affected might have been encouraged to take preparatory steps to enable them to take advantage of this particular provision. These steps might have been begun two months ago, and the delay is especially to be regretted when we bear in mind that there is no legislation requiring amendment in this house before the government could act or before municipalities or industries could seek to take advantage of this provision.

Finally, I think that to require the municipalities to make an application is not in the best interests of the efficient operation of this program. The government should designate on the basis of its own determined criteria what are depressed areas, what are distressed areas and what are areas of chronic unemployment in Canada. I understood from the statement that the onus is on the municipalities to make application. This is an inadequate approach. A couple of weeks ago we were promised that the labour estimates would be dealt with quickly. It is now necessary for them to be called immediately in order that we may examine the details of this plan and see whether it meets the problem.

In this connection, of course, I must say that I, and I am sure all other hon. members as well, feel some sympathy for the British Columbia government with regard to the position in which it has been placed.
All members will be aware that the discussions with British Columbia and the negotiations for the treaty lasted for two years; that in those negotiations British Columbia was fully associated; that the premier and other members of the government of British Columbia made statements from time to time to the effect that as soon as a treaty was signed they would be glad to get on with the Columbia river project, and that the treaty itself was signed with the full knowledge and approval of the British Columbia government. I feel, therefore, that they may have been placed in a rather awkward position by the report of their energy board, in view of the fact that for two years they had given study to this matter, and have made public statements that they were fully in accord with the negotiation of the treaty and wanted to get on with the job as quickly as possible.
For these reasons I think that my comments should be reserved until the position of the British Columbia government with respect to this report is known.

speechtext:
Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the customs tariff and to provide:
1.	That the said act be amended by adding thereto immediately after section 2 thereof the following section:
"2A. (1) For the purposes of this act, goods shall be deemed to be of a "class or kind" made or produced in Canada if
(a)	in the case of goods other than goods custom-made to specifications, goods of approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada; and
(b)	in the case of goods custom-made to specifications adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time.
(2)	Notwithstanding subsection (1), goods other than goods custom-made to specifications shall be deemed not to be of a class or kind made or produced in Canada unless at least 10 per cent of the normal Canadian consumption of goods of the same or approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada.
(3)	The decision of the minister shall be final with respect to the following matters:
(a)	the normal Canadian consumption of the goods described in subsection (2), and
(b)	whether goods are custom-made to specifications, and whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time."
2.	That subsections (9) and (10) of section 6 of the said act be repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"(9) For the purposes of this act, notwithstanding section 2A, goods may be deemed to be of a class or kind not made or produced in Canada where similar goods made or produced in Canada are not offered for sale to the ordinary agencies of wholesale or retail distribution or are not offered to all purchasers on equal terms under like conditions, having regard to the custom and usage of trade."
3.	That subsection (4) of section 6A of the said act be repealed.
4.	That any enactment founded upon this resolution shall be deemed to have come into force on the 21st day of December, 1960, and to have applied to all goods mentioned therein imported or taken out of warehouse for consumption on or after that day, and to have applied to goods previously imported for which no entry for consumption was made before that day.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, from time to time now, over a considerable period, we have returned in committee to this resolution, the discussion of which seems to have caused some impatience in the minds of certain ministers who are, of course, anxious

to get it through. I have no apology to make for contributing, though it will only be for a few minutes, to this discussion.
It has been suggested to us by the Minister of Finance that it is only a small resolution. It is a small resolution but it is one with big implications, implications which extend to the fundamental principle of parliamentary control over taxation. The debate which has already taken place on this resolution has also served to show the historic difference between the two national parties on this whole issue; between a policy of maximum possible trade and a policy of maximum possible protection. No misrepresentation, no distortion of the historical or the contemporary record, can conceal the difference between the two parties in that regard. The record of that difference can be found in the columns of Hansard since 1870.
In earlier parliamentary days there was a straightforward admission of that difference, but now it is not so easy to get exposures by hon. gentlemen opposite of this diversity of approach. Changes are made now, not openly but by subterfuge or, in the language of my hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillin-gate, by adopting a sly and furtive approach to these matters.
Before I outline very briefly our position in respect of the proposed resolution and its effect on our tariffs I should refer to what the Minister of Finance has told us more than once about the purpose of this resolution. Perhaps the briefest definition he gave of that purpose is to be found reported on page 1667 of Hansard of February 2, 1961:
The purpose of the proposed legislation is to restore the original concepts relating to this phrase "class or kind" after what I described yesterday as a decade of erosion. In doing so we will provide for the first time some effective means of dealing with goods that have been described in this proposed amendment.
The minister then said there had been erosion. What presumably is meant by erosion is that the tariff board, the exchequer court and the supreme court have disregarded the intentions of parliament and limited the meaning which successive governments intended to give to the class or kind provision in the customs tariff. We do not agree that this so-called erosion has taken place. The government, we claim, has completely failed to show that any significant difference existed over the years between the interpretation given by the customs administration and by the tariff board. In fact we have shown that in many cases cited by the minister the tariff board has actually upheld the customs administration. I think it is correct to say that in all appeals to the courts from the board, save one, the board was sustained.

The government claims that this erosion began in 1950, but presumably in making that claim they have forgotten that Mr. Hector MacKinnon was chairman of the tariff board from 1940 to 1957, ten years before, and seven years after this erosion is supposed to have started. How then do they explain this sudden change in Mr. MacKinnon? Surely they would not deny that no man better understands the real meaning of the United States-Canada trade agreement of 1935, or the Customs Tariff and regulations, or the meaning of GATT than Mr. MacKinnon himself.
We say there has been no erosion, and that the government by this resolution is in effect asking for power to change the tariff surreptitiously and indirectly, because if it were done directly and openly it would amount to a breach of our international trade agreements. That would be bad enough, but the government does not intend merely to change the law. By this resolution and by action which, it hopes, will be taken in connection with the bill, the government intends to nullify the jurisdiction of the tariff board and the courts and to vest absolute power in the Minister of National Revenue over an important field of the Canadian economy.
It is difficult to get an exact estimate of the amount of trade that would be involved in the application of this amendment, though we have tried to extract it from the minister, I believe, during this debate. It has been estimated that more than $200 million worth of imports would be involved annually and, therefore, a very important sector of our trade would be affected.
The government in this matter is in effect giving the Minister of National Revenue the power to decide without any review or appeal whether the duty on a great number of potential imports

I have used the figure of $200 million-will be high or low. Is it to be 7J per cent or is it to be 22 per cent?
As has been pointed out in this connection, the Liberal government in 1936 clarified the meaning of "made in Canada". It became established that an article to qualify must be made in substantial quantities; and "substantial", as we know, was later defined by order in council as 10 per cent of consumption, with an appeal from that determination to the tariff board and to the courts.
In 1958 changes were made in the dump duty which in many important respects was put under the discretion of the minister. Now the determination of "made in Canada" which is necessary for the application of this dump duty is also to be put under ministerial discretion. From that decision, in respect of certain matters where discretion is given, there is no appeal. There is not even any provision

Customs Tariff
for informing the public when a decision is made, or the terms of that decision. The amendment is perfectly clear on that point. Subsection 3 reads as follows:
(3) The decision of the minister shall be final with respect to the following matters:
(a)	the normal Canadian consumption of the goods described in subsection (2), and
(b)	whether goods are custom-made to specifications, and whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time.
Decision in regard to these matters is given to the minister without appeal and without publicity. Therefore an article in this particular category now becomes made in Canada if the minister determines it to be so, and there is no appeal from that determination. It is this denial of access to the courts, an access which now exists, that is our most fundamental objection to this proposed amendment. I know that the minister in his statements on this matter to the committee has attempted to explain away this denial in terms which he considers to be satisfactory. For instance, on February 27 as reported at page 2460 of Hansard the minister said:
The right of appeal is taken away from no one. The most that can be said-
-and this is a lot-
-is that the right of appeal cannot be invoked on grounds that lie within the three points on which the Minister of National Revenue is given the right to make the final decision.
The right of appeal is taken away from no one, but it cannot be invoked in respect of those three matters the minister mentioned. I consider that mere sophistry. We on this side of the house do not understand how a government which is headed by a Prime Minister who sponsored the bill of rights can justify taking away from the taxpayers the right of access to the courts in matters in which they have enjoyed such access over the years.
If the Minister of Justice were present in the committee I would put this question to him. In any event, I shall place my question on the record. I ask the minister whether he has done what he is required to do, that is examine these particular amendments in relation to the bill of rights. The hon. gentleman is required to do this under section 3 of the bill of rights, which reads:
3. The Minister of Justice shall, in accordance with such regulations as may be prescribed by the governor in council, examine every proposed regulation submitted in draft form to the clerk of the privy council pursuant to the Regulations Act and every bill introduced in or presented to the House of Commons, in order to ascertain whether any of the provisions thereof are inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of this part and he shall report any such inconsistency to the House of Commons at the first convenient opportunity.

I assume that in due course we will get that kind of report from the Minister of Justice which he is required to make under the bill of rights.
That is our basic objection, that the government, in effect, is vesting in a single minister of the crown in certain important matters absolute power to fix the rate of tax which taxpayers will be called upon to pay. We consider that this is arbitrary power. In response to the statement that this is arbitrary power, the Minister of Finance on February 27, as reported at page 2460 of Hansard, replied:
These are not arbitrary powers at all. These are necessary powers in the transaction of the business of this country.
That is another subtle distinction. Our view is that if the rate of tax is to be changed it should be changed in a straightforward way by parliament, and not left to the uncontrolled decision or whim of a minister of the crown as could be done if this resolution were translated into law. We do not think this kind of change is needed at all. We believe it will be not advantageous but detrimental to the Canadian economy, and that by increasing the costs of machinery for production, for instance, it will be particularly harmful to industries which are seeking to expand and modernize in order to improve their competitive position in an increasingly competitive world.
If the government, however, is determined to make these changes in the definition of "goods of a class or kind made in Canada" no doubt its majority will permit it to do so, but we feel we have an obligation to do our utmost to stop the government from taking away the fundamental right of access to the courts which the taxpayers now enjoy in respect of certain matters dealt with in the resolution. No valid reason has been given for denying in future the right of appeal which now exists, and there is every reason for asserting it when it is proposed to give far-reaching powers over the expansion and modernization of industry to a single minister of the crown. That is the basic issue before parliament in this resolution.
We also oppose this measure because it seems to us to be an indirect method of evading our international obligations to our trading partners which is neither honourable, wise nor prudent. Surely if this resolution becomes law it will constitute an invitation to other countries to retaliate against our exports, and the losses to our trade are likely to greatly exceed any small and problematical gains in direct employment.
To sum up, we feel the resolution is wrong. It is dangerous, and should be withdrawn. But if the government will not withdraw it

we appeal to the government to at least abandon its intention of denying the taxpayers the access which they now have to an independent tribunal to review the arbitrary tax decisions made by a single minister of the crown.
Many years ago, Mr. Chairman, a former prime minister of this country and leader of the Conservative party, Mr. Meighen, said, as found at page 3414 of Hansard for 1921:
There should never be an unrestrained discretion in the hands of any minister or any government.
Let me give another quotation from page 4527 of Hansard for June 7, 1955. The paragraph reads as follows:
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that the issue here is deep-seated, clear-cut and fundamental. It is the issue of the rule of law-
We claim that the rule of law is involved in this resolution as an issue.
-and the preservation of the authority of parliament. It is not simply a matter of the preservation ... of the substance of parliamentary authority and rule. We will have nothing to do with the grant of powers vastly in excess of need . . . Supreme over any all-powerful executive, in our view, must stand the authority of a free, sovereign and independent parliament.
Those are good words, Mr. Speaker. They were uttered at that time by the present Minister of Finance. We ask him to apply this principle now to this particular resolution and to bring forward amendments to the resolution which will implement the principles which he espoused so strongly when he sat on this side.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And you opposed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in his closing words the Leader of the Opposition used a quotation from a speech by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen. As I listened to the Leader of the Opposition developing his argument this afternoon, I was reminded of another statement made in this house by Mr. Meighen to Dr. Michael Clark. That statement was:
The hon. gentleman has given us an example of the maximum of merit that a speech may reach without the ingredient of logic or the assistance of facts.
Could there be any words more appropriate to describe all the flurry, fluster and fury which the Leader of the Opposition has just emitted? Perhaps there are some Mr. Chairman, and I will use these to describe what the Leader of the Opposition has said: fanciful, fatuous, fantastic, frivolous and farcical.
What has he done this afternoon in following the lead of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and that of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River is to succeed completely in perverting and distorting the 90205-6-164J
Customs Tariff
effect and significance of this resolution. Indeed, sir, in my experience as a member and observer of this parliament I have never heard such extravagance of language, such intemperance and immoderation of argument, and such fatuity of reasoning as have been unleashed against this resolution. In all the amateur histrionics of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and all the mock heroics of the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon, there has been a total absence of logic, of reasoning. There has been nothing but confusion and distortion.
He is reading every word.
Would the hon. member permit a question? Could he say who wrote that prose?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: This particular hon. member has no difficulty in writing his own prose and in speaking his own prose at any particular time.
Could I ask the hon. gentleman whether he wrote it before he heard the argument of the Leader of the Opposition?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has demonstrated a sufficient number of times on this resolution that his understanding of the issue is in inverse ratio to his volubility.
Let me try to reduce this whole issue to its basic elements and proceed in the simplest terms and by logical steps, I hope, to analyse what is proposed. The first question hon. members must ask themselves is this. Does parliament believe or does it not believe that goods of a class or kind made in Canada deserve a margin of protection in excess of that granted to goods of a class or kind not so made in Canada? If the answer to that question is no, then the matter rests and the committee should defeat this resolution. But if the answer to the question is yes, as I believe it must be, then we must proceed to the next step. How do we determine what is of a class or kind made in Canada?
Hon. gentlemen opposite pay lip service to the principle of class or kind made in Canada but by their words and by their actions they make a travesty of their professions. The fact is that the modern concept of class or kind made in Canada owes its birth to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, to W. S. Fielding and to Sir Clifford Sifton in the anti-dumping legislation of 1904 and later, to the former two, in the tariff revision of 1907. Indeed, in an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press on January 18, 1961, an editorial which was an uninformed and fatuous comment on the speech I made on the supplementary budget, that newspaper claimed that Sir Clifford Sifton himself was

Customs Tariff
the draftsman of the original class or kind legislation; and it was alleged that he did so as an escape from the pressures of the iniquitous Tories of those days who were allegedly seeking a general tariff increase. Clearly, what hon. gentlemen opposite have been doing in following the lead of the Winnipeg Free Press is to repudiate Fielding, to undermine the memory of Laurier and to do violence to the principles which were espoused by Dunning and Mackenzie King.
Let me put the question again, sir. How are you to determine what is of a class or kind made in Canada? As has been pointed out by the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue and as this legislation provides, the answer resolves itself naturally into a division between so-called shelf goods, that is, goods of standard make ordinarily kept in stock, and goods which are custom made to specifications.
I want to deal with them separately. In the tariff there are some 70 items where the rate of duty depends upon whether the goods are or are not of a class or kind made in Canada. Hon. gentlemen opposite, and particularly the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon, seemed to indicate that there were a great many rates that were going to be changed. Actually there are two rates, one rate if it is of a class or kind and one rate if it is not of a class or kind. Of course, as the house knows, section 6 of the Customs Tariff Act imposes dumping duties on imported goods of a class or kind made in Canada if sold for export to Canada at a price less than their fair market value.
Historically, the phrase "class or kind" was broadly interpreted. For over 40 years under a procession of 17 ministers of customs or of national revenue, Grit and Tory alike, the phrase gave little difficulty in interpretation. The broad interpretation may or may not have been correct but at least it has the authenticity of antiquity, the imprint of 17 ministers of the crown. Had there been no change in this interpretation this legislation, or at least the major part of it, would have been unecessary.
The problem of interpretation is clearly set out in Elliott's work, "Tariff Procedures and Trade Barriers", at page 110, from which I would like to quote very briefly:
Many of the classification decisions concerning "class or kind" depend on whether, for the particular articles being considered, that phrase is held to refer to a wide or to a narrow range of goods. Since the Canadian market is small many domestic producers find it convenient to concentrate on producing a relatively few sizes, styles, patterns or types. In some industries the Canadian output is a relatively small proportion of the total Canadian consumption even of the exact types of an article produced in Canada. In more firmly established industries the domestic output forms a large

proportion of Canadian consumption of the exact types produced and, in some, a substantial proportion even of a broader class which includes other substitute products.
There, sir, is the problem and it was met in one way for a period of over 40 years. But in this last decade a new trend has set in, a trend to narrow the phrase. Decisions of the tariff board upset this historic concept. Whether or not these decisions be correct is not the issue. The fact is that the process which the Minister of Finance described as erosion set in.
The best illustration of this is in another quotation from Elliott's book at page 111. I quote:
In allowing an appeal from a decision that certain models of Mossberg .22 calibre rifles were of a class or kind not made in Canada the board cautiously remarked-
This is a quotation from the board decision.
-Dictionary definitions of the word "class" indicates that it is used both for very broad and for very narrow designations, but in the context in which it is used in tariff item 441e it appears to be more or less synonymous with "kind".
Consequently, in interpreting this item the item board has taken cognizance of the more precise designation "kind". Auto-loading rifles are of a kind not made in Canada.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My time is limited, unlike the Leader of the Opposition.

The hon. member can speak as often as he likes. The question I wanted to ask the hon. gentleman was this. Was that a decision of the administration that these were not made in Canada or was it an appeal from a decision that they were not made in Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I quoted simply from the .22 calibre rifle case to indicate what, in effect, the board had done.

This is merely a factual question that I wanted to ask the hon. gentleman. Was the decision of the administration, not of the board, that they were not made in Canada? The hon. gentleman read a sentence relating to that, and if he would just read it again-
What was the ruling of the customs department? Was the customs department overruled by the tariff board?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In this particular case, the tariff board reversed the decision of the department. It is appeal No. 206 of March 17, 1950, and the department was overruled.

The question I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary is, what had been the made in Canada ruling which was compiled by the customs department up to the time of this appeal? What had been their made in Canada ruling, proclaimed for all in Canada to read?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The department held this to be of a class or kind made in Canada. This decision of the department was reversed, on appeal, by the tariff board.
This brings us to the real core of the issue. In effect, class has been interpreted as synonymous with kind. The phrase is not in any way disjunctive; it is wholly conjunctive and the words are synonymous. Indeed, apparently one of them is redundant.
As I have said, 17 ministers of customs or national revenue took a consistent stand for the broad interpretation of these words. Of these 17 ministers, nine were Liberals. There were such men as these. There was William Paterson, Laurier's minister for 15 years. Oh, yes, there was A. L. Sifton; imagine that. There was the unfortunate Jacques Bureau. There were Georges Boivin, W. D. Euler, J. L. Ilsley, Colin Gibson and J. J. McCann. When my hon. friends opposite attack this legislation, what they are doing is repudiating these great Liberals of other days.
That is just nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
They are establishing a counterfeit Liberalism which bears no resemblance to their historic tradition. I say, sir, they are shadowboxing on this resolution and that must cause some of the great Liberals of the past, including the Siftons; Sir Clifford and Arthur L., to turn over in their graves.
They say, you are taking power away from parliament. On the contrary, what we are doing by this legislation is restoring it to parliament. In so far as shelf goods are concerned, the 10 per cent rule was adopted as a result of trade negotiations with the United States. But where did the government of Mackenzie King embed that rule? Need anybody in this committee be surprised to find that it was in an order in council, and not in a statute of this parliament? The policy was: deprive parliament of control, make a mockery of this chamber, keep control in the east block so that at any hour the 10 per cent rule could be suspended, amended, altered, done away with, made 15 per cent or 1 per cent by a simple executive act. This was the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite. This is not the Progressive Conservative way. We are placing it in the statute, so that only parliament can
Customs Tariff
change it. We are doing this in public, and the anvil of public discussion will assure equity to importers and domestic producers alike.
I should like to deal with an argument put forward by the hon. member for Ottawa West. Of all the fatuous arguments advanced, the suggestion that this legislation infringes the rights of parliament is the most ludicrous. It is the very reverse of the truth.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This is balderdash.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate the other day, and the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon, suggested that this legislation violated the bill of rights. Such extreme and immoderate assertions, sir, can only demonstrate how far hon. gentlemen go in substituting abuse for argument and innuendo for advocacy.
I should like to speak of another class of goods, those described as custom-made to specifications. In this field, each product is unique or virtually unique. If one goes back over the 50 years of history of class or kind or, I am told, if one reviews the statements over those years of the ministers of customs and of national revenue, although I have never had a chance to do so personally, it is clear beyond peradventure that it was never intended by any government that custom-made goods should automatically be ruled as not made in Canada. Yet this is the direction in which the rulings of the department and of the appellate tribunals have gone.
In carrying out the intention of parliament in respect of this class of goods, obviously there must be a broader ministerial discretion than is necessary or appropriate in relation to mass produced or shelf goods. Surely, if parliament has any interest in promoting the manufacture of goods in Canada, the tests proposed by this legislation are reasonable. The tests are that adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time. Each of these phrases, sir, is capable of simple, rational interpretation. I cannot, for the life of me, see how the competent officers of the customs division, and they are highly competent and skilled, will have any difficulty in interpreting in these words what I believe has been the intent of parliament over the years.
I should like now to deal with what the Leader of the Opposition suggested this afternoon was, in effect, the nub of the problem. I refer to the question of appeal from a ministerial decision. I want to suggest to the committee that all the confused argument has been based upon a false premise, namely the premise that the right of appeal from an administrative act is a natural right. The fact is-

Customs Tariff
It is an existing right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The fact is that there is no inherent right of appeal except such as may exist indirectly through the prerogative writs.

We have had it for 25
years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I will deal with this directly if my hon. friends will only be quiet for a moment. The right to appeal is a right which must be conferred by statute. The fact is that there are very few administrative acts of government that are subject to any appeal whatever. Every day, and every hour of every day, ministers of the crown as well as other public servants take important and vital decisions which are subject to no review-
Such as setting tax rates.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: -except by this parliament. My hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillingate sits in his seat and interrupts, but he is too learned an historian-
I would be very happy to stand up and ask the question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will answer the questions later.
I was going on to say that my hon. friend is too good an historian, and too skilled in the art of government to believe that the right of appeal is the rule. The fact is that it is the exception rather than the rule, and even to be an exception it must be statutory. I should like to refer to the case of Okalta Oils Limited v. the Minister of National Revenue, (1955) Supreme Court Reports, page 824. At page 825 Mr. Justice Fauteux said:
A right of appeal is a right of exception which exists only when given by statute.
This places the matter in perspective, I submit. There is, of course, always the judicial review by means of a prerogative writ such as mandamus, prohibition and certiorari, or the statutory writ of habeas corpus.
Let me turn now to the type of review which has been conferred by statute in the past in respect of customs matters. When, under the Laurier government, the modern concept of class or kind made in Canada was initiated, the determination of class or kind was the responsibility of customs appraisers, subject to review by or appeal to the board of customs.
The board of customs was the final appellate tribunal. This was the tribunal which existed, and the only tribunal, throughout the whole of the Laurier administration and the whole of the first Mackenzie King administration. Sir, what a great appellate tribunal it was. If my hon. friends will look at the

revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, they will find that it had five members: the commissioner of customs, the assistant commissioner of customs and a third, a duly qualified officer of customs, designated by the governor in council. Out of the five members three were customs officers. Then, to get the right degree of objectivity, the other two were the commissioner of excise and the commissioner of income tax, officers of the same department after it became the Department of National Revenue in 1927.
That was the type of appellate tribunal in which the Liberal party believed. From 1904 to 1931, the final court of appeal in respect of class or kind, lay within the department itself. In effect, the department reviewed its own decisions. What a happy, happy situation.
Behind all the utterances of hon. gentlemen opposite those are the facts. If they dare open its pages and examine the report of the royal commission on the customs scandal of 1927-dark pages in the history of Liberalism .-let them read what Chief Justice Brown had to say about this technique of review, and how he recommended it be changed to a board of national revenue. Did the government of Mackenzie King change it? No, they left the respondent as the judge and jury.
Who was it that changed this situation? It was the man for whom hon. gentlemen opposite still reserve their most severe strictures. Changing this was part of the so-called iniquity of the R. B. Bennett government. It was that great Canadian, so slandered and vilified by hon. gentlemen opposite, who sought from parliament the right to create a tariff board which would be a court of record, assuming the quasi-judicial functions of the board of customs and exercising as well the fact finding and advisory powers formerly possessed by the advisory board on tariff and taxation or the so-called Billy Moore board.
It was the Conservative party under the maligned R. B. Bennett which placed appeals upon a proper and legitimate basis.
Perhaps the hon. member would tell us-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman just possess his soul in patience?
The committee may be interested in knowing how the Liberal government jettisoned all appeals to the tariff board for a period of four or five years. The story is told in Alex Elliott's "Tariff Procedures and Trade Barriers" to which I have already referred. At pages 60 and 61 it reads as follows:
The terms of two of the members expired in 1943 and the Board no longer had a quorum of two members. Accordingly, until the board was reconstituted the system of informal appeal within

the Department of National Revenue became even more important and was more fully developed. Departmental officials express pride in this informal, cheap, and speedy method of appeal.
So that we see, sir, that over the years the actions of the Liberal party have been very different-very different indeed-from their professions of these last few days, or indeed these last few weeks, from the bombast that the committee has heard and been forced to endure.
The house may be interested in one further quotation from Mr. Elliot's book in respect of appeals. At page 59 Mr. Elliot says this about the enactment of section 43A of the Customs Act in 1937.
At the same time the door was closed to appeals for refunds of duty previously exacted by inserting a new section (43A) which validated all official valuations that had been made and confirmed the duties collected under them.
I repeat, sir, the door was closed to appeals.
We now see how genuine, how real are the professions of my hon. friends opposite. Not only were they content to take away the right of appeal, but they retroactively deprived prospective appellants of rights which had vested. I suggest they be judged by their acts and not by their expostulations or their professions.
Now, sir, are there statutes where the right of appeal having once been conferred, has been abridged or limited? From July 1, 1954, to June 21, 1957, my distinguished historian friend from Bonavista-Twillingate was the minister of citizenship and immigration and the committee is entitled to assume that he has greater familiarity with the Immigration Act than any other act. Having that overwhelming instinct for reform which he now seems to display, what did he do to amend the appellate provisions of that act? I will mention to the house just two sections. Subsection 4 of section 31 reads as follows:
The Minister may in any case review the decision of an Immigration Appeal Board and confirm or quash such decision or substitute his decision therefor as he deems just and proper and may, for these purposes, direct that the execution of the deportation order concerned be stayed pending his review and decision, and the decision of the Minister on appeals dealt with or reviewed by him or the decision of the majority of an Immigration Appeal Board on appeals, other than those reviewed by the Minister, is final.
Section 39 reads as follows:
No court and no judge or officer thereof has jurisdiction to review, quash, reverse, restrain or otherwise interfere with any proceeding, decision or order of the minister, deputy minister, director, immigration appeal board, special inquiry officer or immigration officer had, made or given under the authority and in accordance with the provisions of this act relating to the detention or deportation of any person upon any ground whatsoever, unless such person is a Canadian citizen or has Canadian domicile.
