speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have just indicated that the hon. gentleman was the minister of citizenship and immigration during this time.
The hon. gentleman has directed a question to me. I do not know whether he wants an answer to it. I will be pleased to supply one if he wishes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will have plenty of time to reply later.
I have said only that the hon. gentleman during this period of years did nothing about this situation.
That statement is untrue.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Let us examine the records of this house and we shall see.
I deal now directly with the allegations against the appeal sections of this resolution. If one were to listen to what the Leader of the Opposition said this afternoon one would conclude that the tariff board had been ousted completely. That is the impression he sought to leave, and indeed, Mr. Grant Dexter has said so directly in the Winnipeg Free Press, although he must know how erroneous he is.
The fact is that in all material particulars the right of appeal is preserved intact and such abridgement or limitations as are provided are in lesser particulars, largely of a statistical nature. Such limitations, sir, are commonplace in statutes providing the right of appeal, whether it be the Supreme Court Act or in the provisions for lesser appeals.
In respect of shelf goods, hon. gentlemen seem to say that the one important issue is to determine the normal Canadian consumption and that all else is a mathematical calculation. That is not right at all. The really vital issue or the central problem of all is this. Are the goods in fact of a class or kind made in Canada? On that issue, and it is the vital one, the regular appeal procedure is preserved intact. The regular procedure of appeal remains unabridged in respect of the determination of the amount of Canadian production and in the application of the ten per cent rule. The abridgement relates only to a statistical computation in respect of which the opportunity for error is virtually nonexistent.

Customs Tariff
My hon. friends have exclaimed that an unscrupulous minister could cook this statistical computation. Any attempt at impropriety would be known to this House of Commons within 24 hours and the real sanction of this high court of parliament would come into play.
The argument in this respect would really carry one to the impossible result that no final administrative decision could be entrusted to a minister of the crown. Indeed, that is exactly what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said, as reported at page 1722 of Hansard.
I said no such thing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Then I will read to the hon. gentleman what he said on that occasion:
I say that every administrative decision affecting the rights of a citizen should be subject to an appeal
The rights of a citizen, yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: All administrative decisions involve the rights of a citizen.
"Appeal" is the important word.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: If such were the case, we would not have government; we would in effect have a state of anarchy. I think it must be evident to all hon. members of the committee that hon. gentlemen opposite, prodded by the Winnipeg Free Press, are pursuing their old strategy of playing both ends against the middle-I use that expression both literally and figuratively-in regard to tariff policy. They blow hot and cold; they beat around the bush; they straddle the fence.
All at the same time?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Let me just illustrate my point. If you look at page 571 of Hansard of February 1, 1960, you will see that my hon. friend from Ottawa East (Mr. Richard) is in favour of the total elimination of tariffs on automobiles from the United States. Yet every member of this house knows that the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) favours almost prohibitory restrictive measures against the importation of automobiles and automobile parts.
What justification is there for that statement?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member for Essex East favours sky-high tariffs for all the products of Essex county and free trade for the products of every other county of Canada.

I think the hon. member for Essex East, who has been very noticeable by his silence in this matter, should enter this debate before it is finished and tell the committee what he finds objectionable in this legislation. He has been voluble on other subjects, but he has been noticeably silent on this matter.
I have never been one to believe that to say "raise a tariff item" is to utter naughty words, any more than I am prepared to believe that one instantly surrounds oneself with a halo of righteousness when he says "lower tariffs". My philosophy in this is purely pragmatic. In this day, one cannot be theoretical. It is not really a question of tariffs at all; it is purely a matter of classification, of what will contribute to employment and development in Canada without prejudice to our export trade. In that I believe. This resolution meets that test and on that basis should have the support of the house.
I say to hon. gentlemen opposite, let us be done with silly, political manoeuvring, with the hollow sham of the type engaged in by the Liberal front bench, seeking only to resurrect the political quarrels of yesteryear and doing damage to secondary industry and employment in Canada, as well as to primary producers, east and west alike.

Mr. Chairman, I am not rising to speak; I am merely rising to correct an incorrect statement made by the hon. member for Carleton who has just resumed his seat.
The hon. member said I had done nothing whatsoever about the appeal provisions of the Immigration Act. Of course, the hon. member, from the phrase he read, made it very clear that those provisions did not, in fact, in any case apply to Canadian citizens at all. They could not apply to Canadian citizens at all. They apply only to persons who are not Canadian citizens.
However, since the hon. gentleman has taken it upon himself to make this statement, I should like to remind the committee, that in fact I prevailed upon the governor in council to exercise the powers given him under that act to set up an appeal tribunal for landed immigrants and to give every landed immigrant a choice between having his case dealt with finally by appeal board or by the minister.
If the law had allowed me to do so, I would have made it absolutely final; but the law as it then was, did not allow me to make it absolutely final. I also stated on more than one occasion that on the first occasion I had the opportunity to make any suggestions in parliament for changes in the act, I would suggest that this appeal jurisdiction be made

final. But I went just as far as the law, which the Minister of Finance helped to enact, allowed me to go. It was made before I came into this house, and I went as far as I could to assure appeals even to landed immigrants.

Mr. Chairman, for the past 40 minutes I have been sitting in my place listening with awe, fascination and admiration to the outflow of words from the hon. member for Carleton. Over the years I have heard members overcome with the exuberance of their own verbocity, but the hon. member gets the championship in this respect. It was absolutely awesome to follow the flow of adjectives and connotations in his opening remarks when he was trying to get in what I presume was a good offensive, or defensive, with the heavy guns. I thought his words were so wonderful that anyone who followed the hon. member should at least for one sentence try to reply in kind.
I know I can never meet the verbiage of my hon. friend, but I would like to say that in my opinion his remarks were such a vapid, vituperous, vitriolic, vindictive, vilifying, venting from a vacuum as has been seldom heard in this house. Mr. Chairman, I ran out of "v's".
May I in all sincerity say to the hon. member that the way to influence members and win friends and support is not by bombast; it is not by riding roughshod, but by trying to put forward in a calm and deliberate manner that which will answer the objections raised on this side of the house.
Whether the government likes it or not it must be recognized that there is a great deal of concern in Canada about the implications of the matter which is before us through this resolution. Very, very definitely there is major concern in western Canada.
When I spoke on this resolution on February 2 I tried to set forth what was causing concern to the primary and manufacturing industries of British Columbia and the boards of trade. I pointed out at that time that the primary and manufacturing industries and their organizations, and we too, are very seriously concerned about the word "approximately" used in the phrase "goods approximately the same class or kind made in Canada". I pointed out that we thought that if what we took to be the meaning of the minister in his opening remarks was correct, it would go a long way to satisfying those who are disturbed if that section of the proposal were to read, "in the case of goods other than goods custom-made to specifications, goods of the same class or kind similar in nature and purpose made or produced in Canada".
Customs Tariff
I spoke at some length on this matter on February 2. The minister was good enough to reply in such a manner as to, in his estimation, clarify the situation. I wish to draw the attention of the committee to certain parts of the minister's statement on February 2, as reported at page 1684 of Hansard. The minister said, as reported in column 1:
I hope I can convince him.
That is, myself.
As I have said to those organizations which made the recommendations from British Columbia,
I think their fears are based on an assumption and I do not think the assumption is warranted. In general I think their fears have been greatly exaggerated.
The minister continued:
I shall be glad now to give to the committee and to the hon. member the substance of the views which have been conveyed to these associations. The concern which they have expressed is to the effect that there will be a material increase resulting in the cost of machinery and tools of production used in their operations and thus their position in relation to export sales will be weakened.
The minister then went on to try to clarify the situation. He spoke at some length, and, as I say, I appreciate that. On the following day, without any comment from myself, I sent a copy of Hansard containing the hon. gentleman's remarks to those organizations in the producing and manufacturing industries which had brought this matter to my attention in the first place. After studying the statement of the minister together with the information he had supplied, these people came to the conclusion that they have even more reason to feel concerned at the present time than they did before. As a result, they are in outright opposition to the proposals now before us.
I know that at least one body has made additional representations to the minister. I refer to the Vancouver board of trade which, apparently, takes a view similar to that taken by many of us here. The longer this debate goes on and the more time we have to study this question, the more concerned we are becoming about the possible effect of the changes in the Customs Tariff in connection with the "made in Canada" rulings which the government proposes to introduce.
So, once again, I have to ask the Minister of Finance whether he can clarify the situation further in the light of these new representations following a study of the statements he made in this chamber on February 2. I should like the minister to say whether or not he can answer the problems which these people foresee and whether he can give them assurances that the government proposals will not mean increasing costs in British Columbia. It is still my opinion,

Customs Tariff
which is reinforced by this recent information, that the legislation we have before us now is, at least, so controversial that it should definitely not proceed until a great deal more study has been given to it by those who will be affected.
I should like in particular to draw the attention of the minister to five points which, in the opinion of British Columbia, are of major concern. They are outlined in a letter to the minister from the Vancouver board of trade. The first of these five points read as follows:
(a)	The phrase "custom-made to specifications" is ambiguous because it does not state whose specifications shall be considered. Many custom-made goods are bought on the manufacturer's specifications subject to modifications by the customer. It is suggested the wording should be clarified and provision made for the securing of rulings in advance.
The second point reads:
(b)	The words "adequate facilities" seem to mean that a "Made in Canada" ruling could be secured before there is in fact any manufacturer in Canada. Otherwise Canada will be in the anomalous position of having something declared to be "Made in Canada" which has never in fact been made in Canada.
The third point is also very important. It is:
(c)	The words "economic production" are not satisfactory because it is not clear to whom the test of economic production is to be applied. Further, if a Toronto manufacturer is declared as having adequate facilities for the economic production within a reasonable period of time for a Toronto customer how does this affect a Halifax or Vancouver customer? Is freight to be a consideration? It is conceivable in the above example that a Toronto manufacturer could be economic to a Toronto buyer and not at all to a Halifax or Vancouver buyer. If freight is to be a consideration then should not the legislation say so?
The Toronto case is, of course, given as an example. That is how they feel in British Columbia, and I agree with them. Then, again, the point is made:
(d)	The words "reasonable period of time" are not satisfactory since what is a reasonable period for the manufacturer may be completely unreasonable for the buyer.
Finally, the board states:
(e)	The minister's determination may take place at a time when there are outstanding orders with foreign manufacturers. It is departmental practice to acknowledge the problem of "lead time" but there is no guarantee that such practice will be continued when discretion in the matter is vested in the minister without right of appeal. The buyer who had orders outstanding at the date a ruling was made by the minister should be specifically protected in the legislation.
There we have in general the views which have been expressed to the minister. These are the reasons why they are still concerned in British Columbia about the possibilities and the implications of this legislation. I do not intend to take time in order to express their

attitude, and my own, with regard to the question of appeal. I think sufficient has been said on that subject already. Anyway, the bombastic arguments used on the government side and the sneers directed against those in the opposition who try to present the situation as they see it, and as they understand it from outside, are not going to resolve these doubts in any way.
I wish to say this. From all the communications I have received, from discussion with my colleagues and from my own studies to the best of my ability I believe that if the proposals now before us become legislative enactments established as regards the made in Canada rulings under section 2(a) 1(a) and under section 2a (lb), there is every possibility-indeed, it is almost inevitable-that the effect at least in western Canada will be to limit our ability to produce in order to be able to compete on world markets. That ability means everything in my province of British Columbia. I feel that costs of production in western Canada and in Canada as a whole are already too high and that the passage of this resolution will worsen the situation. I think it would be especially harmful to the maritimes and to the province of British Columbia.
I have tried to express the views of the primary and manufacturing industries of British Columbia as well as of the board of trade as they were relayed to me. Perhaps I do not understand this problem but surely industry does. This was their feeling which I expressed on February 2 and it is their feeling now. After reading the words of the minister on this subject there is an increasing feeling that this is dangerous to Canada and harmful with respect to maintaining the position of industry in western Canada.
I am always open to conviction. Although much time has already been spent on this resolution I hope the minister will take a little more time in order to answer the questions that have arisen. If the hon. gentleman does not do a better job of explaining than he has up to this time it is the opinion of many in this chamber and of industry in western Canada that the only course open to the minister is to withdraw the legislation for further and continuing study.
But doing nothing, most of the time.
The government has done this at a time when the decision is appealable. If it is not appealable the government can change it every week or two and we cannot do anything about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to interrupt the hon. gentleman but if he wishes an answer to his question, I can give it to him if he would prefer to have it now.
The hon. member should be allowed to embellish his argument without interruption.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was just asking the hon. gentleman if he wished the answer now or later. I am prepared to give it now. The answer is very simple, Mr. Chairman. The generator the hon. member speaks of was not made in Canada in 1959 but by 1960 it was being made in Canada.
On the 10 per cent rule?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

In view of the minister's explanation I should like to ask him a question. The generator came in free of duty in 1959. Would the minister extend the same advantage to, let us say, the premiers of Quebec or New Brunswick

gentlemen of different political persuasion-if they wanted to bring one in this year? It seems likely that if Mr. Bennett of British Columbia goes up to the Peace river to build a generating station he might be in the market for a generator. Would the same advantage be extended to him if he wanted to bring in a generator.
Not the Peace river, but the Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The law is uniformly applied but the hon. member must appreciate that at times new products are manufactured in Canada. If one happens to be of the kind we are discussing here then obviously a time comes when an article that was up to that time ruled to be of a class or kind not made in Canada thereafter may be ruled to be of a class or kind made in

Customs Tariff
Canada. These situations change. That is what happened in the case to which the hon. member has just now made reference.

Does the minister then say that the generator of the type and size that was imported by Canadian Fairbanks Morse in 1960 was not of a class or kind made in Canada and would the same apply with respect to the hydro generator?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, let me make this clear. The hon. member uses the words "type or size". I have said, in the language of that statute, that the generator that he speaks of was, in 1959, not of a class or kind made in Canada but that by 1960, because of manufacture in Canada, it was in 1960 of a class or kind made in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, would the minister inform all of us what in 1960 made the change? Which manufacturers were providing the 10 per cent or perhaps the equivalent that is necessary under the law?
Surely the minister is going to answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, but I am not sure that I should give names in a situation like this. I happen to know what the names are. I have just received information from my advisers. I do not think the hon. member is going to ask for names. The information is that the manufacture of this type of generator was being carried on in Canada in 1960. I would not mind giving the hon. member the information he requires but not the names.
I do not want the names.

I should like to ask the
minister whether this generator that was imported in 1960 would be regarded under the present law as shelf goods or as custom-made goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The latter.

If it was possible to determine that an article of this sort, which the minister said was custom-made goods, had been made in Canada in 1960, can the minister then explain why the present amendment he is asking for is necessary at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member is talking about one case but we are talking here about all cases in relation to some 70-odd items of the tariff. The hon. member has simply picked out an illustration of the fact that the situation can change, that an article that is not at some particular date made in Canada can be made in Canada at a later time, and therefore the change almost

automatically follows under the statute and the article, if imported, then attracts a higher rate of customs duty.

Before the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River proceeds, I might point out that the parliamentary secretary told us this afternoon that the erosion had gone to such a point that custom-made goods were automatically ruled not to be made in Canada, so whom do we believe, the minister or the parliamentary secretary?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With respect, Mr. Chairman, let us keep this discussion on the rails and close to what hon. members have been saying. I have made my remarks about the erosion and I am not repeating them at this time. The fact is, however, and everybody is aware of it, that when the manufacture of an article is introduced in Canada, if it is introduced in sufficient quantity then the case moves from one of goods of a class or kind not made in Canada into the category of goods of a class or kind made in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, throughout this debate the Minister of Finance has made what I regard as a specious and improper argument when he has said that the rates of duty are not affected by the amendments before us. On the sole basis of interpretation of language I could agree with him but with respect to the effect in an industrial way we have had many comments during this debate as to what might be involved so far as volume of trade is concerned. The Deader of the Opposition referred to a figure of $200 million of trade imports in this particular arena. That figure, of course, cannot be taken as a maximum because we have to have regard for things that probably were normally produced in Canada and as a result the figure could be terrifically high.
In this debate I think the Minister of Finance has continually avoided a proper answer to the questions we have raised on some of these matters. Certainly there is nothing in what the Minister of Finance calls a short, simple resolution that changes the rates of duty. The hon. member for Vancouver East has been vocal in this debate but I hope that members of parliament from the prairie provinces, who happen to be all on the government side with the exception of the hon. member for Assiniboia, and Conservative members from the maritime provinces will tell us whether they have studied the implications of this resolution and whether or not they have decided that they approve of the resolution. They have been slavishly silent and have been of completely no help to us with regard to these matters.

I think the time has come for members of parliament from these areas who support the government to tell us whether or not they have studied the uncertainties that have been suggested by the opposition. The things that we have suggested are likely to be very adverse not only to consumers and end users but to the possibility, as the hon. member for Vancouver East mentioned today, of new industries in British Columbia in that this legislation, by means of an unnecessarily high impost on the cost of their basic machinery, will increase their costs to the extent that they will not be efficient. I believe these things have to be considered and in my opinion there are many subjects to be discussed in connection with this resolution.
There is the question of our relationships with GATT. There is the question of whether or not the historic concept has been properly presented by the Minister of Finance. I assert that it has not been properly presented to the house by him. I ask the minister at this point to have regard to the situation vis-a-vis GATT. We are all rather uninformed. We are not specialists or experts in this highly complicated field involving trade amounting to perhaps $5 billion or more.
Normally we rely on a minister to come before the House of Commons and, regardless of his political responsibilities, to accept the administrative responsibility to tell all of us in this chamber what we want to know. We expect that of a minister. We do not want quick assertions such as he made in a speech in Toronto when he said that the action of the government has aroused the interest of all our associates in GATT and that the government is confident that what they are proposing to parliament is within the framework of GATT. Members of parliament, I think, usually pay attention to language such as that used by the minister in addressing laymen in Toronto on January 9 when he said that "our proposals have aroused interest". Surely there is a warning to every member of the House of Commons to ask questions with respect to the use of a loose phrase of that type.
I want to know whether or not the minister is prepared to comment upon his responsibility in connection with the alteration of our trading law that is involved in this redefinition as it relates to article X, subsection 3, paragraph (b) of the general agreement on tariffs and trade signed at Geneva, October 30, 1947, by Canada and many other countries. I quote from this section of the agreement:
Each contracting party shall maintain or institute as soon as practicable, judicial, arbitral or administrative tribunals or procedures for the purpose, inter alia, of the prompt review and correction of administrative action relating to customs matters.
Customs Tariff
I speak only as a member of this House of Commons, and I do not claim to be a lawyer interpreting this provision. I think it is written in laymen's language. In my opinion, it means that the contracting governments will maintain an appeal opportunity that is above and beyond its customs administration. Of course, prior to the signing of this agreement we had such a procedure in Canada. This meant nothing to Canada.
However, despite the eloquent remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Carleton, I suggest that the obvious elimination of appeals in certain areas of customs matters is certainly a violation of this section of the agreement which we made with so many other trading countries in 1947.
I know that the government asserts that our courts have, in some way, in the last decade eroded the situation that existed when we signed this agreement. This particular subject has been debated in this committee on four or five occasions, and on each occasion we have challenged the Minister of Finance, and those who speak for officialdom, to tell us in what respect our partners in GATT can consider that they received what he described as free or non-traded benefits. I do not believe that the minister or his parliamentary secretary has indicated to this committee where we have been giving away, through our judicial processes, something that was not expected in 1947.
I want Canada to retain the things in the agreement that were to Canada's advantage when the agreement was signed in 1947. This administration has not indicated to us in any way that we are not being placed in jeopardy of retaliation in so far as our export industries are concerned. This new proposal is, in fact a departure from what was contemplated by all our trading partners in 1947. I want the utmost for Canada, of course, but what I am afraid of is that, by passing legislation of this kind, we are going to get reprisals, perhaps in a subtle way, from our trading partners. No member of this parliament will hear a word about it, but our exporters will suffer. Our representatives who sit in Geneva year after year, clever and able though they are, are going to be embarrassed by the legislation that is proposed here.
As hon. members of the committee are aware, I have a question on the order paper on this subject. I was rather loath to put it as a formal question, but I wanted to ask this government to inquire about protests that may be received by our representatives at home and abroad. I refer, of course, to people who might feel that, under the terms of the GATT agreement, they were entitled to

Customs Tariff
certain adjustments in the trading arrangements that were outlined in part I of the schedule to the agreement. I regret, Mr. Chairman, that I had to put this question in Votes and Proceedings, but I feel that the minister is so glib that I would not ask him this question. I followed this procedure deliberately because the minister has been too glib in the debate and not too accurate in his information to the committee.

I did not intend to enter the debate again. I spoke a few days ago. However, I should like to say that I resented the attitude of the opposition frontbenchers in taking the floor from my good friend the hon. member for Welland. I was enjoying the remarks of the hon. member for Welland and I would have been pleased if he had been given the opportunity of completing his remarks. Perhaps he was saying the wrong thing. He certainly was expressing the principle set out in the resolution we are discussing now. In fact, I do not believe he could do otherwise because he comes from an area in which there is a great deal of secondary industry.

I am very glad the hon. member for Lincoln intervened in the debate at this point because otherwise I might have forgotten a point he made the other day in debate and to which I want to refer. I am very grateful to him for reminding me of it.
I want principally to speak about the speech made this afternoon by the hon. member for Carleton who apparently thought that rhetoric and bombast would be an adequate substitute for a total lack of substance, because there was an almost total lack of substance in his speech. I think we would all have been much more impressed if the hon. gentleman in talking about erosion had given us examples of erosion.
As I understand it the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Revenue and now the parliamentary secretary, claim that the nature of this erosion has been that the tariff board and the courts by their decisions have changed the concept of a class or kind made in Canada from what it was ten years ago, and have narrowed it and limited it in a way in which it was not narrowed and limited ten years ago. If that is not a correct statement of what erosion means according to the minister, I would be happy to be corrected, but I think it is.
I have examined every one of these seven cases that the hon. gentlemen have adverted to, but they have been very careful to see to it that we are never given particulars. Even the hon. member for Carleton, when referring to the case of the .22 rifles, seemed to be singularly lacking in detail. I have

here a few details about that case which I think ought to be placed on the record because it is typical of all seven that I have examined in somewhat more detail in private than the hon. gentleman did in public.
In the case of the .22 rifles it is true that there was a decision of the deputy minister that these rifles, of a particular kind, were of a kind made in Canada, but I am informed, and I think quite correctly, that these rifles were not ruled of a class or kind made in Canada in the customs memorandum, series D, No. 51 MCR 14, then in effect at the time this decision was made. That memorandum had not been cancelled. That memorandum I might say, constituted the decision of the commissioner of customs, Mr. H. D. Scully, that the seven models and makes of the .22 calibre automatic rifles were of a class or kind made in Canada on April 11, 1939. In other words that decision of the tariff board was a decision that was in line with the decision made by Mr. Scully in 1939, which the deputy minister departed from in his decision of 1949. The plain fact is that the deputy minister, by his decision, had enlarged what had been the historic concept. The tariff board has properly gone back to that historic concept in every case that I have examined.
Of course the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River mentioned the undisputed details of the shovel case which showed that over the years the shovel case was decided in one way and on an appeal in the way the department had decided over the years and then the deputy minister made a different decision, which was overruled by the tariff board which again went back to the historic concept.
If we had time, sir, we could go through all these cases and show that in every case there was in fact no erosion at all. We could show very much the contrary, that the tariff board and the courts followed the historic trend consistently. What is more, it does seem to me that my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River in reading the provision of GATT, drawing to our attention article 10, has given indication that this is so.
Article 10, section 3 (b) reads as follows:
Each contracting party shall maintain, or institute as soon as practicable, judicial, arbitral or administrative tribunals or procedures for the purpose, inter aba, of the prompt review and correction of administration action relating to customs matters.
Mr. McKinnon was chairman of the tariff board for seven years before 1947 and for ten years afterwards. I do not think anything happened suddenly to Mr. McKinnon which would make him erode the decisions he had himself made. Everyone knows that Mr. McKinnon was one of the principal architects

of GATT. Everyone knows that Mr. McKinnon knows better than anyone what GATT meant. I do not think anyone really would be expected to believe that Mr. McKinnon would make decisions that were contrary to GATT.
I would suggest, sir, that this attempt by the government to take away many of the essential elements of appeal to an administrative tribunal is a clear infraction of that section of GATT. It is a deliberate attempt to disregard the provisions of our international obligations.
The parliamentary secretary this afternoon jeered at the reference made by the Leader of the Opposition to the bill of rights. I would just like to draw to the attention of this committee the terms of section 2 (e) of the bill of rights which reads as follows:
(e) deprive a person of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice for the determination of his rights and obligations;
No one could deny that at the present time these decisions as to whether an article is of a class or kind made in Canada, are appealable to the tariff board on all the elements and facts of the case, and not on selected facts, selected by the ministry, while other selected facts are to be excluded.
The minister said this afternoon that this was not a determination of the rate of duty, but that is precisely what it is. When the minister makes one of these class or kind decisions he is determining the rate of duty. The minister can arbitrarily and finally, in the case of custom-made goods, and also' by jiggery-pokery, if he wants to exercise his powers in the case of shelf goods, make an arbitrary decision which cannot be appealed, and in the case of normal Canadian consumption, one taxpayer might be paying 22 per cent and the other 7 per cent in comparable circumstances from which there can be no effective appeal.
No one knows about it.

As the member for Kenora-Rainy River said, it is done in secret. It may be perhaps done by someone other than the minister himself. As everyone is aware, most of these decisions are made by clerks and not by the minister at all.

Would the hon. member permit a question?
Just before he sat down the hon. member said that most of these decisions were made by clerks. I take it we can assume that he himself made a number of decisions for Mackenzie King.

No, I did not make any decisions for Mr. Mackenzie King because
Customs Tariff
neither Mr. Mackenzie King nor myself happened to be the Minister of National Revenue or a clerk in the department at that time, and that is what we are talking about now. I think there is plenty of scope within the ambit of this resolution to keep us busy without going off into that kind of diverting diversion, if I may put it that way.
Like British trade.

Yes, like British trade as the hon. member so aptly puts it. Why is the government so frightened of the tariff board? This is a tariff board that they themselves appointed, and yet they are so anxious to take jurisdiction away from the board. That is what they are doing; they are taking away from the tariff board the jurisdiction it now has in the determination of whether a man's obligation is to pay the lower or the higher rate of duty. They are taking away the right a man now has to have a determination by a tribunal.
Why does the government want to do that? Why are they afraid of their own board? What do they think the board is going to do? That is why I was glad the hon. member for Lincoln intervened in this debate because I might otherwise have forgotten this point. The hon. member for Lincoln really let the cat out of the bag the other day. He told us it was not easy to get at the tariff board, but it was easy to get at the minister. That is the reason, and that is the only reason that makes any kind of sense.
I know the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister of Finance, and today the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance, have given the reason that every tyrant has always given for discretion; that it is faster; that it is more efficient; that they are good tyrants anyway. They say, "Maybe the wicked Liberals would do things badly, but not us good Tories. We would assure justice for our friends, and the Liberals do not deserve any justice anyway".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is bad grammar. Change "us" to "we" there.

I know it is bad grammar, and it is bad law that the minister is trying to enact. No doubt one bad thing tends to generate another. That is exactly the gravamen of my argument.
Why do they want this arbitrary power? What secret, clandestine purpose have they in mind? As the Leader of the Opposition said earlier today, if the government insists on putting in this bad definition and using its majority, a majority from provinces that are going to suffer very seriously because of this law, of course we cannot stop them. But at least it will be the law and at least there

Customs Tariff
will be tribunals to determine the matter. But they insist not only on changing the law; but they say there can be no appeal and a taxpayer cannot get the new matter before the courts.
In his omniscient wisdom the Minister of National Revenue will decide these things. They say that it does not matter anyway, that these things are very easy to decide. If they are easy to decide, what difficulty is there about sending them to the tariff board for decision? Moreover, the Minister of Finance, on December 20 in the debate on the supplementary budget, said this as reported at page 1013 of Hansard:
-we consider it important to provide for careful investigation and public hearings before major tariff revisions are introduced. This permits all interests and all points of view to receive full consideration. We believe that the tariff board is the appropriate body to undertake this task, and that in order to do so expeditiously the board should be enlarged sufficiently to permit it to adopt a panel system.
In other words, the minister himself in his speech on the supplementary budget said that the tariff board was the appropriate body to decide these questions. Why does he not let the tariff board decide them? It is true the minister said at another point- and I am not going to the trouble to look it up, unless I am challenged; I have the reference here-that there had been a welter of these appeals; but the Minister of National Revenue said there had been very few. Since they are appeals from the decisions of the Minister of National Revenue, I suppose he really knows better than does the Minister of Finance how many there are. If there are very few, it will not clog up the work of the tariff board to decide them. If there are many appeals, it would suggest there are many taxpayers who feel they have a right to take seriously the words that the Prime Minister put into the bill of rights through this parliament, namely that a person should not be deprived of the right to a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice in the determination of his obligations.
What is a tariff? It is a tax. In this legislation we are saying that the Minister of National Revenue shall decide what the tax is to be, instead of parliament so deciding. As a result of this legislation the Minister of National Revenue will decide whether it is to be a low rate of duty or a high rate of duty.
If custom-made goods are concerned, nobody can challenge that decision at all; there is no way of going beyond it. If shelf-made goods are concerned, all the minister has to do is fix the normal Canadian consumption at such a figure whereby it can be

shown that 10 per cent is produced in Canada and there is again no appeal.
In other words, the meaning is taken right out of the right of appeal. It is true that one can appeal on some of the facts, but the board is not allowed to look at the rest of the matter. They will therefore be incapable of making any decision that has any meaning. This is a travesty of justice.
As the Leader of the Opposition said, this is the fundamental problem. We do not like this surreptitious method of trying to increase the tariff, but that is a proper difference between the two parties. If hon. gentlemen opposite want to do that, they have a majority and all we can do is make our arguments in parliament, put up the best case we can and let the house decide. But when it comes to this question of a fundamental right to a hearing that was supposed to have been guaranteed in the bill of rights only one year ago, we think that surely sincerity should be shown in the very first case to come before parliament and the provisions contained in the bill of rights should be put to the test.
We say that the Prime Minister should come to this committee and tell us why he thinks it is necessary to take away the right of appeal which now exists. He should tell us why it is taken away from people with regard to many important, and indeed what could be decisive facts, when it is necessary to decide what tax people are to pay and what rate of tax is to be imposed upon them.
We think the Minister of Justice should tell us why it is so essential to brush the courts aside, because forsooth the Minister of Finance says that the courts have eroded the law. If the courts have eroded the law- the minister thinks, as he always does, that repeated assertion makes something a fact- he has given us no facts to demonstrate this.
When I asked the minister the other day to cite one case where the rulings of the customs department have been reversed by the tariff board over the years, he dodged the question and he keeps on dodging it. This is simply making a travesty of the bill of rights. It is making a travesty of the rule of law, and of course it is seeking to take away from parliament and hand to the minister the arbitrary, final power to decide what one taxpayer shall pay and what another taxpayer shall pay, without anyone else being able to look at the case at all.
That is what we in this committee are being asked to approve in this resolution and to found legislation upon. I say, sir, that no more fundamental issue could come before us. Not only is the jurisdiction and

the right of parliament to impose taxes being eroded-that is what the minister is seeking to do-but the right of the taxpayer to a fair hearing and to justice is being eroded. We think these two fundamental principles are the most important, though we do not deny the importance as well of this back door method of trying to increase the tariff.

Mr. Chairman, this debate has been going on for a long period of time.
I am sure the minister and his officials are getting a bit weary. Still, I believe that if he is getting worried and upset over the delay and the long period of time which has been taken, that is one of the penalties he has to pay for attempting to impose upon parliament by this method the right to give a minister of national revenue the unqualified and unappealable powers which this resolution seeks to confer. This, in my view, is the first and only matter to which we should direct our attention at the moment. It is with regard to this issue that some sensible, logical and reasonable explanation-if there is any- should be made. Following the removal of this final and arbitrary power which is being sought in the resolution we should be in a better position to discuss the other effects of the changes proposed in so far as the economy of the country is concerned.
Speaking for myself, I say this. Unless we can have from the minister sponsoring this resolution some indication that he is prepared to alter paragraph 3 relating to the finality of the minister's decision, unless we can obtain some admission that the hon. gentleman has made an error and that he really does not wish to confer on his colleague in the government authority and power of this type, I have no intention of supporting the other proposals which go along with it.
As the hon. member for Bonvista-Twillin-gate pointed out a short while ago, toward the end of the last session, with all the trumpeting and fanfare attendant upon a circus, we passed the bill of rights. Presumably we thought that this bill of rights meant something. We took the word of the Prime Minister and others that it meant something and that it would have some baring upon conditions such as those now being sought by the Minister of Finance. However, it is quite obvious that the government really had more verbosity than integrity when it proposed and introduced the bill of rights last session because what we have before us now to my way of thinking, is completely contradictory to the principles contained in the bill of rights and absolutely at variance with the speeches which the Prime Minister and other gentlemen made about rights and freedoms during the last session, in other sessions, and over the years. In addition, it is contrary in my
Customs Tariff
view to all the concepts we have grown up with in this democracy regarding the desirability of removing arbitrary powers from the hands of one or two people in high positions.
For countless years people in this country and in other countries have rebelled against the concentration of authority and power in the hands of one or two persons. The Conservative party, when it was over here on this side of the chamber in opposition, was notable for its objection to the extension of the emergency war measures powers which were wanted when Mr. C. D. Howe was in office. They claimed then that these were arbitrary powers intended to be placed in the hands of one person, that it was shocking to ask for them, and that they should not be continued. The longer this sort of thing goes on, the longer the Minister of Finance and others seek to repeal some of the concepts of democracy and freedom and replace some of the concepts of the bill of rights by a back door approach-I was going to use a word there which came immediately into my mind, but I got into trouble with that a few weeks ago, so I had better not use it again; I will use the word "left-handed"-or a left-handed approach and seek to abridge these freedoms which have taken hundreds of years to develop, they are displaying propensities which are nothing short of tyrannical-and we know that the Minister of Finance is perhaps not lily white in this regard.
I cannot for the life of me understand why the government wants to have these authoritarian powers or why it should want the right to make decisions in secret in some room and not have those decisions brought into the light. I cannot understand why it does not wish them to be subject to an appeal to some other agency or authority such as that which exists in our courts of law. I cannot, as I say, understand for the life of me why they should want this sort of dictatorial power unless there is something nefarious about it, and I am not suggesting there is. I am suggesting, though, that we have so far not received from the Minister of Finance any reasoned or logical explanation as to why he should want his colleague to become more of a dictator than is possible under our present system.
No matter how far the government has convinced itself that it is gentle and kind and sweet and lovable, no matter how far it has convinced itself that it is going to make the right decisions and be generous to everyone and preserve the rights and freedoms of the people, the fact remains that the more that power is concentrated into fewer hands, the easier is the step towards tryranny and dictatorship and the greater is the desire to remove that remains of the freedom and rights

Customs Tariff
of the people. One of these rights is the right to appeal decisions reached in secret behind closed doors by politicians when heaven knows what sort of pressures are used to get them to make particular decisions. We know that cabinet ministers, like other members of parliament, are subject to pressure from time to time. Some of this pressure is political, and some types of it are worse than others. Some are of a minor nature involving, say, a problem connected with unemployment insurance. But we know there are pressures from certain forces in the economy which would like the government in office to enact laws or regulations which would benefit some small group to the detriment of everyone else. These pressures exist whether the government in office is made up of Conservatives or whether it is made up of people having any other political conviction.
I think the Minister of Finance is being extremely unkind and unfair to his colleague or to anyone else who might hold the office of Minister of National Revenue by seeking to give him power and authority of the kind proposed in this resolution. Ministers of the crown are political figures upon whom more pressures are brought to bear than upon private hon. members by way of telegrams, briefs, letters, telephone calls, personal visits, requests and so on. In giving a minister the type of power sought by this resolution we are placing him in a position of being increasingly subjected to political pressures and requests for determinations under this proposal which might be to the advantage of some segments of the economy and to the detriment of others.
The problem is lessened if the minister is strong-willed, determined, courageous and honest but if he is vacillating, weak, dishonest or unscrupulous the danger becomes very real. This has happened in the past. Not long ago in British Columbia the minister of lands and forests found himself in a difficult position. A minister with a lack of integrity and honesty may be unable to resist the pressures exerted and he may agree to make a determination in return for one of a number of considerations or for a variety of reasons. The decision is unappealable and cannot be reversed. The decision of the minister is final with respect to those matters enumerated in this resolution.
I have no intention of granting this authority to any minister, regardless of who may be holding the portfolio. I say that with all due respect for the present Minister of National Revenue. We are not dealing here with the personal qualities of the minister but with the government's resolution.
I will not support a resolution that can lead to the possibility of a power-mad

minister, perhaps not long in office, not bothering with the cumbersome difficulties of processing appeals through other bodies but preferring to make decisions in secret behind closed doors, possibly in response to political pressures or pressures that will provide income to the party coffers.
From time to time editorial writers and politicians level accusations against the socialist movement charging that the socialist movement advocates state control. This is true. Many charges are made against the socialist movement by those who like to make a play of the principles for which we stand. Politicians may do this in an attempt to gain political advantage. Never in their wildest dreams, however, would those who make accusations against the C.C.F. think of accusing the socialists of seeking what the minister now seeks in this proposal, namely individual ministerial control which will lead to the whittling away of our democratic institutions and the undermining of our democratic concepts.
The hon. member is right. It worries the Liberals.

I did not hear that observation. I am prepared to sit here day after day while the Minister of Finance attempts to justify his request for tyranny, dictatorship and authoritarian control, but I have no intention of supporting this proposal. If it is possible for the minister to be humble perhaps he will tell us he does not really seek this power and will have one of his colleagues move an amendment granting the right of appeal. If that is done, I will withdraw my opposition, the amendment may be proceeded with and I will support it.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide among other things:
1.	That with respect to income of corporations earned on and after January 1, 1961, the amount of the first bracket of taxable income subject to a rate of tax of 21 per cent be increased from $25,000 to $35,000.
2.	That for the 1961 and subsequent taxation years the additional tax of 4 per cent imposed on investment income of individuals be repealed as applied to income from sources in Canada.
3.	That for taxation years commencing in 1963 and subsequent taxation years a corporation will qualify as an investment company only if not less than 75 per cent of its gross revenue is received in the form of dividends from taxable corporations resident in Canada and that for taxation years commencing in 1961 and 1962 this requirement be 55 per cent and 65 per cent respectively of such gross revenue; however, this requirement shall be 75 per cent of such gross revenue for taxation years commencing in 1961 and 1962 in the case of a corporation that received not less than 75 per cent of its gross revenue in the form of dividends from taxable corporations resident in Canada in its taxation year that commenced in 1960, and 65 per cent of such gross revenue for taxation years commencing in 1961 in the case of a corporation that received not less than 65 per cent but less than 75 per cent of its gross revenue in the form of dividends from taxable corporations resident in Canada in its taxation year that commenced in 1960.
4.	That for taxation years commencing in 1963 and subsequent taxation years a trust or corporation established or incorporated solely in connection with, or for the administration of, a registered pension fund or plan shall be exempt from tax only if 90 per cent of its income from investments is from sources in Canada and that for taxation years commencing in 1961 and 1962 this requirement be 70 per cent and 80 per cent respectively of such income; however, this requirement shall be 90 per cent of such income for taxation years commencing in 1961 and 1962 in the case of a trust or corporation that received not less than 90 per cent of its income from investments from sources in Canada in its taxation year that commenced in 1960, and 80 per cent of such income for taxation years commencing in 1961 in the case of a trust or corporation that received not less than 80 per cent but less than 90 per cent of its income from investment from sources in Canada in its taxation year that commenced in 1960.
5.	That the exemption from the 15 per cent tax payable by a non-resident person on interest received from a Canadian resident, now granted for interest payable on bonds of or guaranteed by the government of Canada, be repealed with respect to interest on bonds issued after December 20, 1960, other than bonds held by
(a)	national governments of foreign countries and their central banks, and
(b)	such international agencies as may be prescribed by regulation.
6.	That the reduction from 15 per cent to 5 per cent in the rate of tax payable by a non-resident person on interest received from a Canadian resident, now granted for interest on bonds or other obligations of or guaranteed by Her Majesty in right of a province, and for interest on bonds or other obligations provision for the payment of which was made by a statute of a provincial legislature, be repealed with respect to bonds or other obligations issued after December 20, 1960, except bonds or other obligations issued after
Income Tax Act
December 20, 1960 in respect of which a written agreement was formally entered into on or before that day for the purchase and sale, in specified amounts and at specified prices of all of the bonds or other obligations included in the issue.
7.	That the exemption from the 15 per cent tax payable by a non-resident person on interest received from a Canadian resident, now granted for interest payable in a currency other than Canadian currency, be repealed except for
(a)	interest on any obligation where the evidence of indebtedness was issued on or before December 20, 1960,
(b)	interest on any bond or similar obligation issued after December 20, 1960 in respect of which a written agreement was formally entered into on or before that day for the purchase and sale, in specified amounts and at specified prices, of all of the bonds or similar obligations included in the issue, or
(c)	interest on any obligation incurred in the course of carrying on a business in a country other than Canada.
8.	That the reduction from 15 per cent to 5 per cent in the rate of tax payable by a non-resident person on dividends received from a Canadian resident, now granted for dividends paid to a non-resident corporation which owns all the voting shares (except directors' qualifying shares) of the Canadian resident paying corporation, be repealed with respect to dividends paid after December 20, 1960.
9.	That the rate of tax payable by a non-resident corporation on dividends received from a Canadian resident, now limited to 5 per cent in accordance with paragraph 2 of article XI of the income tax convention between Canada and the United States be increased to 15 per cent with respect to dividends paid after December 20, 1960.
10.	That with respect to income earned on and after January 1, 1961 a special 15 per cent tax be imposed on a non-resident corporation carrying on business in Canada, other than a bank, life insurance company, transportation company or communications company and that the tax be computed by reference to the amount remaining after deducting from its taxable income earned in Canada the aggregate of
(a)	the tax payable under part I of the Income Tax Act, including the tax payable under subsection (5) of section 10 of the Old Age Security Act,
(b)	income taxes payable to a province which are not deductible in computing income for purposes of the Income Tax Act, and
(c)	an allowance in respect of net annual increases in its capital investment in property in Canada.
11.	That where the contractual rate of interest on any bond, debenture, mortgage, note, bill or similar evidence of indebtedness issued by a tax-exempt borrower including a government after December 20, 1960 is less than 5 per cent, and the evidence of indebtedness is issued at a discount which provides an effective yield to maturity, or to the earliest call-date, that exceeds the contractual rate by more than 33£ per cent thereof, the whole of the discount shall be deemed to be income in the hands of the first Canadian resident taxable holder of the evidence of indebtdness.
12.	That for the 1961 and subsequent taxation years a student in full-time attendance at a university in a course leading to a degree be permitted to deduct in computing his income the tuition fees paid by him in the year to the university, and that the said tuition fees also be deducted in computing the income of the student for purposes of determining whether the student is a dependent.
