speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
with respect to the income tax resolution may I suggest that as it is one resolution with 12 paragraphs we follow the procedure of other years, that you call the paragraphs separately as though they were separate resolutions and that we adopt them seriatim in the order in which you call them.

Mr. Chairman, if I understood the minister correctly he suggested that the paragraphs of the resolution should be called seriatim. I think it has been the usual procedure to have some discussion about the resolution as a whole before individual items have been called and I would hope that procedure could be followed. That is the procedure we would wish to follow at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say something on this matter because in former years we have had a discussion on the resolution as a whole. I find, in going back to June 4, 1956, that after a discussion of the income tax resolution that covered 24 pages in Hansard the hon. member for Greenwood said, "We have been all over creation", and the hon. member for Eglinton then proceeded to make a speech that took up another six pages. I think we should have an opportunity at this time to discuss the income tax resolution in a general way rather than proceeding to discuss the paragraphs seriatim. After the dinner recess on the occasion to which I have referred there was discussion of the sales tax and the excise tax. The hon. member for Eglinton at that time discussed such matters as the excise tax on furniture and shoes. He said that members of the house should rise in angry indignation against a government that would dare to maintain a 10 per cent sales tax on shoes and furniture and yet the tax is now 11 per cent. I think we should be granted the same privilege as the chairman of the committee at that time granted the hon. member for Eglinton.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Do X understand it is the wish of the committee to discuss the resolution as one resolution and pass it as one resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it would be the wish of the committee to have an orderly discussion and the subject matters of the 12 respective paragraphs of this resolution vary quite widely. Unless we arrange to call each paragraph separately as has been
[The Deputy Chairman.]
done in other years, I think we are going to have a very discursive, mixed up and unsatisfactory discussion.
One hon. member opposite, at any rate, indicated that he wished to say something in general. He then proceeded not to talk about the Income Tax Act at all but about the sales tax which has nothing whatever to do with the Income Tax Act. We are not back to the budget debate. Anything that is relevant to any of the paragraphs of the resolution can be said, of course, with respect to each of them, but this is not a warrant for talking about the sales tax.

Since this is one resolution, I think it would be our wish to have a certain amount of discussion about the whole resolution and I think we would be quite agreeable after that discussion to follow the suggestion of the Minister of Finance that each item should be taken seriatim. This is a single resolution and under the rules, therefore, we have a right to discuss it as a whole. We would like to do that for some little time at the beginning.

Mr. Chairman, when the minister introduced his so-called baby budget shortly before Christmas the only reference he made to the most important domestic problem in our country, namely, unemployment, was when he indicated that he proposed to provide for the application of the concept of double depreciation to what he called chronically unemployed areas. Since that bare announcement some two and one half months ago there have been persistent interrogations from the Liberal opposition addressed to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Prime Minister as to when we might expect a more detailed statement about this proposed policy.
When the policy was announced there was some expectancy in the country that this kind of relief, if embodied in a real plan, might provide some mitigation in certain surplus employment areas, and thereby give these areas some relief from the serious problem of unemployment that attended them and has attended them since this government came into office. However, in spite of our interrogations of the ministry from time to time we were never able to ascertain which department of government was responsible for the administration of this policy. We also were not able to ascertain what kind of criteria would be invoked by the government to determine which areas could qualify for the beneficial consequences of the policy which the Minister of Finance announced before Christmas.

Not only were we unable to elicit any information but we were led to believe by the Minister of Finance that there could be no announcement of the details of the policy designed to meet the serious emergency of unemployment until such time as the budget resolutions had been disposed of in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
That is what the Minister of Finance told the hon. member for Laurier early in the month of January.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member please direct his attention to the words I used. I said, until the house had passed upon them. I referred to the adoption of the main motion to resolve the house into committee of ways and means. I did not at any time say until after the resolutions had been adopted in committee of ways and means.

The Minister of Finance is entitled to his interpretation of his own words and I am entitled to place my interpretation upon them. The record is clear. He indicated to the hon. member for Laurier early in the month of January that it was not possible to announce the number of areas that were going to be included in this plan for assisting the chronically unemployed sections of the country until such time as the budget resolutions had been' passed. The minister also told the hon. member for Laurier that a member with his experience should know that was the case. He was naturally assuming that there was no provision in the existing law which would prevent any other course being followed than that outlined in the response of the Minister of Finance.
However, as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River pointed out a few days later, we had been misled by the Minister of Finance. I shall be kind to the minister and say that he likely forgot the provision in the existing Income Tax Act, which enables the executive to make a decision to provide for the application of added depreciation, if such decision is taken by the governor general in council. There can be no justification, in the face of this situation, for the long delay we have had at the hands of this government in giving to the house and the country even a semblance of the criteria, which the government intends to invoke in the application of this proposal for double depreciation. As a matter of fact, we are not even now acquainted with the facts as to whether or not the government has acquired for itself, pursuant to the Income Tax Act, the necessary power to implement the vague announcement made today by the Minister of Labour.
On orders of the day this afternoon we sought to ascertain from the Minister of
Income Tax Act
Finance whether or not an order in council has been passed which would permit the implementation of this new policy of the government which, by the way, is intended to operate not for a period of years but for one year only. The Minister of Finance, for reasons best known to him, refused to say positively today whether or not the cabinet had in fact acted in the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I did not do any
such thing.

We have the anomalous position of a reluctant Minister of Finance seeming to be unwilling to disclose whether or not the government had, after two and a half months, acted in this matter.
The announcement made by the Minister of Labour today, welcome as it is and to the extent that it goes, has not been clothed with any legal authority whatever in so far as this committee knows. Undoubtedly the governor in council could meet tonight, or perhaps it did meet between orders of the day this afternoon and this period tonight, and could have taken the necessary steps pursuant to the Income Tax Act, to acquire the necessary power to authorize the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Labour, who apparently now is being charged with responsibility in this matter, to implement the program announced a long time ago.
Why the government has waited so long to implement what, at least in principle, is a constructive approach to the solution in part of the problem of unemployment is difficult to understand. One can only suggest it is because this government is used to postponing decisions and to delaying action, and has once again forgotten the assurances that it gave not only to parliament but to the people of Canada in the budget which was introduced by the Minister of Finance shortly before Christmas. The fact is that this program will be implemented long after the event, although we were called here in November to deal with certain emergency legislation, designed mainly to deal with the problem of unemployment in the long term along with this scheme which is designed to deal with unemployment forthwith.
The fact is that this government did dedicate itself to the solution of the unemployment problem when it appealed to the people in 1958, but it has waited over 2J months before announcing the details of a plan that would give to municipalities and to corporations some indication of the kind of relief which the government intended. The government, therefore, stands indicted by these delaying tactics, this laissez-faire attitude and this lackadaisical manner in whcih it has

Income Tax Act
approached the problem of unemployment in our country. One can only compare this anaemic approach to this serious domestic problem with the attitude taken by the government of the United States. That government has not hesitated to state the character of the problem. It has not hesitated, through its chief executive, to lay before congress proposals which are designed to meet this problem.
Half of which we have already carried out.

One method which the United States proposed was the application of this principle of double depreciation for the assistance of what are called in that country, unashamedly, distressed areas. In this country the Minister of Finance takes exception to our referring to these surplus areas of unemployment as "distressed areas". He calls them chronically unemployed areas. I do not know what difference there is between a chronically unemployed area and a distressed or depressed area. The fact is that, in the chronically unemployed areas and in the distressed or depressed areas, we have the picture of thousands of men and women out of work.
Many of those who are out of work are in a very unhappy position because they have exhausted their unemployment insurance benefits and their right to supplementary payments under the Unemployment Insurance Act. They stand in need of assistance to the extent that it is provided by the municipalities, the provinces and this government under the public assistance program that stands on our statute books.
Let us compare the situation in the United States in this particular with the situation that we have today as a result of the vague announcement made under duress by the Minister of Labour. First of all, the Minister of Labour has announced that assistance will be given under certain criteria, and that areas will be divided into two groups, those with a labour force of more than 10,000 and those with less. Areas with a labour force above 10,000 must have been classified as labour surplus areas for 75 per cent of the 48 summer months, that is from May to October, between 1953 and 1960. I call the attention of the house to those years. They must also show a decline in industrial employment during this period. Those areas with a labour force below 10,000 must have been classified as labour surplus areas by the Department of Labour for half of the summer months between 1953 and 1960, and these areas must also show a general depreciation in employment.

The areas involved may either correspond to areas served by a national employment service office, or with the boundaries of a municipality. But we have this mere outline, which the Minister of Labour was content to accept as criteria and which was hastily devised, because yesterday we learned for the first time, from the Prime Minister which department of government was going to be responsible for this matter. It will not be forgotten that last Thursday we asked the Minister of Finance who was going to be responsible and we got from him a characteristic reply that revealed nothing. Then the Minister of Trade and Commerce disclaimed any responsibility, although this kind of program in the United States and in Great Britain is carried out under the administration respectively of the secretary of state for commerce in the United States and the president of the board of trade in Great Britain. We learned yesterday from the Prime Minister that the responsibility was going to lie with the Minister of Labour.
From the conduct of the ministry during these last few days under our interrogations I suggest that it was not clear under which department the responsibility for this matter would come. It is clear from the conduct of the ministers that the Minister of Trade and Commerce was to be charged with part of the responsibility. But, because of the reply given yesterday by the Prime Minister when I asked him which minister was to be in charge and he replied the Minister of Labour, it obviously became necessary for subordinate ministers to foregather and decide either in cabinet or among themselves, that the Prime Minister could not be let down, and that the responsibility in fact must now be entrusted to the overworked, overburdened, over-concerned Minister of Labour.
That is the situation. It is no wonder then that we learned from him today details so vague in character as to convey no real information to anyone in this country in regard as to what are the real criteria. The fact that the government has not adopted the criteria being used in the United States or in Great Britain is, of course, of no real concern apparently to the government. The government today in its announcement did not indicate what areas or what communities of the country could possibly benefit from this program. The Minister of Labour charged with this responsibility, sitting now on the treasury benches, when confronted with this situation said: "I ask the member for Essex East to say now whether or not the city of Windsor is to be designated as a distressed area," as though that was my responsibility, and as though I had concocted

this weak infant, this new instrument by which the government hopes to combat the problem of unemployment in Canada.
I have no hesitation in saying that Windsor certainly is an area which should receive at the hands of this government the benefits of any kind of program that will encourage industry to stay in the community, and will encourage industry to locate in that area in the hope of mitigating the problem which only now the Minister of Finance is beginning to recognize as really existent in this country at this time.
The Minister of Finance?

I did not mean to say the Minister of Finance. I must not put too many responsibilities on the Minister of Finance whose burdens now are obviously more than he can bear.
The Minister of Labour today in announcing this program refused to indicate what communities in Canada could in the opinion of the authors of this plan benefit from it. He would not tell us how many communities were covered. That was something that could be determined by hon. members opposite. That was something that could be determined by the member of parliament for Essex East himself, in so far as his own community was concerned. But to let municipalities in Canada know what the government proposes to do for them, that was not the responsibility of the government of Canada. He said in effect, let the municipalities themselves examine this proposal which I make; let them examine the criteria, and if they think that their situation comes within the embrace of our criteria then they can make application. That was an unfortunate attitude for the Minister of Labour to take in the face of this serious problem.
I say to the government that the responsibility which is on it to designate forthrightly the areas in Canada that it regards as coming within the category of a chronically unemployed or distressed area is one that should be recognized by it immediately. Let it say positively that Elliot Lake, Spring-hill, Cornwall, Peterborough, Windsor and other communities in Canada are areas which fall within the criteria instead of leaving this to surmise and guesswork. Our municipal officials are going to have a great deal of difficulty in analysing what this statement really means unless they are now going to be assisted by the research that the Liberal party has done in trying to interpret for the Minister of Labour what in fact his resolution really means.
Income Tax Act
It would seem from what the Minister of Labour said today that some 11 communities in Canada may possibly come within the reach of this proposal for a system of depreciation. The minister has referred to Elliot Lake. I doubt whether, under the formula as he gave it to the house, Elliot Lake, ably represented in this house by the Leader of the Opposition, could properly qualify. No one I am sure will deny that the unemployment problem in Elliot Lake is such that it should be one of the communities in our country to benefit from this kind of proposal, which is very limited because it is to be extended only for one year.
The areas which, according to my interpretation, fall in this category-and I give this information for the benefit of these communities in Canada because the Minister of Labour refused to do so-seem to be Brantford, where the percentage of unemployed in the required period is 90.5 on the basis of the last available figure for 1959; Windsor, with 80.9 per cent; Rouyn, Val d'Or, with 76.2 per cent; Shawinigan, with 90.5 per cent; Cornwall, with 80.9 per cent; New Glasgow with 80.9 per cent; Lac St. Jean, with 76.2 per cent; Three Rivers, with 90.5 per cent; and Saint John, New Brunswick with 88.1 per cent. Then referring to the minor areas

two in number-they are Newcastle, with 85.7 per cent unemployed and Drummondville, with 78.6 per cent. That list of names does not include Springhill and does not include Elliot Lake.
I suggest to the Minister of Labour that if he carefully analyses what was prepared for him, he will find that the two examples he gave of communities capable of qualifying for this assistance are communities that will be denied this assistance under the very plan which he announced to the house today.
Have we not reached a sad state in this country, when the government, through the Minister of Labour, in the announcement of a plan has been reluctant to say which communities in Canada can in its judgment qualify for this assistance? That is exactly the position we have had portrayed today by the very limited announcement made by the Minister of Labour. The minister is in the best position to give us this information. The unemployment insurance offices in Canada are administered by the Minister of Labour through the unemployment insurance commission. He is the minister, above all ministers, who has the information which alone determines whether or not a particular area comes within the compass of this particular proposal and is to receive the benefit of the double depreciation allowance.

Income Tax Act
It is difficult to understand why the minister is reluctant to give this information, except that it is in keeping with the attitude of this government from whom we have had to extricate information as though we were pulling teeth from the strongest jawbone of the strongest organism known to man. We have had to do that in order to elicit the kind of information which we feel the people who are suffering from unemployment in our country are entitled to have.
When one examines this particular proposal of the Minister of Labour, one finds certain conditions that perhaps require a great deal of explanation by the minister, and I hope he will give that explanation tonight. Let us examine the proposition of these two categories. First, areas of 10,000 or more. The ratio of applications for employment on file with the national employment service of paid workers, including those looking for work, according to this plan must have exceeded (a) 6 per cent in industrial areas of 25,000 or more for 75 per cent or more of the 48 months from May to October, 1953-60; and (b) 7 per cent in areas below 25,000 and above 10,000 for 75 per cent or more of the 48 months from May to October, 1953-60. Second, industrial employment must have declined over the period 1953-60.
I would like to remind the committee of one thing at this juncture. The basis for the figures, according to the Minister of Labour, that are going to be used is not the dominion bureau of statistics' figures but the figures of the national employment service. For two and a half years we have argued in this house that the real measure of unemployment was something approximating the number of people in receipt of unemployment insurance and the number of unplaced applicants; that is, the N.E.S. figures. The government has said that these were the wrong standards to use. We were told at the end of last session that the government was going to resort to a new formula. We were later told, before we reconvened in November, that the new standard of measurement of unemployment in Canada was to be one standard, the dominion bureau of statistics' figures.
Yet in the announcement made by the Minister of Labour today, he used the N.E.S. figures, thereby upholding and confirming the position which we in the Liberal party have maintained throughout the last two and a half years. If it is satisfactory to use the N.E.S. figures now, why is it not satisfactory to use those figures along with the unemployment insurance figures to determine the real state of unemployment in our country?
On the basis of the D.B.S. figures we are told by the government that some 693,000

people in the month of January, the last reported period, were out of work. If we are to add to that the numbers included in the standard used by the minister in his statement today, we would certainly be presented with a much higher figure.
With regard to areas below 10,000, the ratio of applications for unemployment on file with N.E.S. of paid workers, including those looking for work, according to the minister as I interpret it, must have exceeded 7 per cent for 50 per cent or more of the 48 summer months May to October, 1953-60. Industrial employment conditions likewise must have generally deteriorated over the years.
This is not the whole story. The minister has said nothing about the major agricultural areas of our country, where unemployment exists in very large numbers. According to his announcement today, agricultural areas are not included-

Mr. Chairman, I begin my remarks with an apology. Unfortunately we have not the services of the "Martin B.S." and we have not the statistics in relation to what communities or areas are going to come under this emergency legislation. But I must say I was disappointed, while listening to the hon. member for Essex East, to find that the Port Arthur-Fort William region does not seem to qualify for this particular type of assistance.
To talk about the Port Arthur-Fort William region may seem parochial at this particular stage, but I think what is taking place there in so far as concerns unemployment, and the structural developments in the whole employment picture, is typical of other places in Canada and certainly implies a very strong criticism of these proposals not unlike that made by the hon. member for Essex East. Whether or not we are a distressed area, the communities, including the two municipalities of Port Arthur and Fort William, have undertaken an employment survey of their own, supported by their own funds, and using local people. They had the advantage, through the kindness of the Minister of Labour, of the advice of Department of Labour economists. They are in the middle of a study of our employment situation.
In several months' time they will have a report analysing why our unemployment has skyrocketed very much in the last three years. It seems to me that the basis upon which the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour are approaching this matter of what is a distressed area or an area that is going to receive the advantage of these taxation allowances is a most unfair one.

I can explain that best by analysing the unemployment structure in our particular area, which has been of a very high level especially since 1956. We have a very high income level in the region of northwestern Ontario. I think it is one of the highest in Canada. But we have also had an increase in the last three or four years of a very marked unemployment problem. The reasons for this relate to the very nature of the industries.
We have three basic industries, transportation, pulp and paper and mining. I do not know of three industries anywhere else in the nation in which there has been more capital input, more productive gain and the creation of fewer job opportunities. I can give illustrations of this in the pulp and paper industry, where they can now cut twice as much wood as they could ten years ago, with the same labour force. Yet the full effects of all the mechanization in the woods and in the pulp mills, all the dieselization on the railways and the modern loading facilities at elevators, and all the improvements in mine machinery and techniques that have made it much easier to get a ton of ore up from the bottom of the mine, are only now really crystallizing and having their effects.
Our crisis has come upon us very suddenly. It was masked to quite an extent by the expansion in the last few years of the service industries. We have now just about as many bowling alleys, motels, barber shops and service centres as can be supported at this time by our basic industries. Yet if you are going to base this assistance through the tax act and tax concessions upon a look into the past back to 1953, you are not going to get a true picture of the crisis which our area faces. In other words, the whole of this legislation is based on a statistical look backwards to 1953.
It is apparent that the department is thinking in the terms that it is summer unemployment which gives you the real indication of the danger to a community. I insist that is wrong, and one of the reasons it is wrong in areas such as ours is that in the last five years there has been a complete transition in our employment pattern. Where once most of the wood was cut in wintertime, now it is cut in the summer and fall months. That transition would not be noticed at all by the statistical pattern that is going to be invoked in relation to this kind of assistance.
The Minister of Finance himself when he introduced in his budget speech pointed out the limitation on what you could do through these depreciation allowances. It still remains to me to point out that he has scuppered the whole project by the way in which it is going to be applied. I insist just as strongly 90205-6-165
Income Tax Act
as the hon. member for Essex East representing Windsor may do that we have a crucial situation at the head of the lakes. If ever there was an area which needed assistance in terms of any kind of allowance for depreciation, it is ours and yet that fact is never going to be revealed from the statistical analysis which is necessary.
There is one other point I want to make clear. I fail to see what the federal government is doing in asking municipalities to deal directly with it and to inform it of their situation. What kind of an informal relationship is this when we have the traditional pattern in Canada of the municipalities, if not being the creatures of the provinces, at least in all their relationships with the federal government going up through the provinces. Surely that is the chain.
I cannot myself understand where the provinces fit into this picture. I know that Premier Frost, despite his political party, has a better understanding of our problems in northwestern Ontario than this government seems to have. He knows we have a crisis up there. He knows what has happened to industries of ours such as the Port Arthur shipyards and the Canada Car factories at Fort William. I doubt if we shall ever build another ship in the Port Arthur shipyards on a commercial basis in view of the changes which have taken place in the conditions of shipbuilding in this country and in the world generally. Yet it is apparent that this government has forgotten those promises, despite the kind words it gave us two years ago through the Minister of Public Works when he was so sympathetic, and so anxious that our big Canada Car plant should carry on. Here we have a huge plant which is now down to a level where 200 men are working in it though it has a capacity in terms of space and equipment to employ several thousand. We have a shipyard which has been working at a capacity of between 20 per cent and 25 per cent. Surely these are the very kind of industries which need this assistance; yet what hope is there under the formula we have had today?
I cannot claim to have understood the formula fully. There may be some loopholes which would enable us to sneak in, but I should like to suggest to the Minister of Finance that on the surface, on a quick interpretation, these concessions are not going to do my part of the country a single bit of good. I hope there are a good many members of parliament irrespective of party who recognize the same thing with regard to these income tax changes and who will get up and inform the Minister of Labour that this is not good enough.

Income Tax Act
There is one section of the income tax change which is extremely welcome. I must compliment the minister for broadening this provision since he made his initial presentation with relation to education allowances. I should like to know from him whether nurses are included under his heading of technical education in regard to post-secretary school training. That is not clear to me. Certainly where nurses have had a grade 12 education, generally matriculation is considered the completion of secondary level. In many parts of Canada they go on and train on a full-time basis for three years. It costs their parents in many cases a great deal of money even though there has been a trend to paying them a small amount of money as spending money. I think we would be very much indebted to the minister if he would indicate that nurses qualify for this particular provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I may deal with that question now though we shall be considering it when paragraph 12 is before us later. I should think that nurses attending a nursing school on a full-time basis where the course is open only to graduates of a secondary school would qualify.

I am very pleased to hear that. There is one other thing which is not a matter of interpretation and I think it is regrettable. I am noticing that many of the witnesses who are appearing before the Senate committee on manpower are stressing the need for people after they complete their normal education to carry on with their own development themselves. It has always been the attitude of the income tax authorities that this post-graduate training that they do in part time and spare time increases their capacity or ability to earn more revenue, so the expenses they incur in acquiring this education have never been recognized as deductible for tax purposes.
I wonder whether the minister has not considered that he could give a fillip to both summer training and academic, technical and vocational training of many kinds if he were to provide that seriously undertaken part time training for a graduate degree or for extra vocational training of a journeyman kind could be considered for deduction. It seems to me this is one of the incentives which we could give to a great many people in Canada to improve their talents or improve the position and the ability of the whole labour force of Canada.
The more complex parts of the income tax amendments are beyond my capacity to criticize or to make any suggestions about, but I would reiterate to the minister that it is most disappointing that the indication

in the statement we have had today from the Minister of Labour is that this is going to do so little for so many parts of the country which know they are in a crisis situation in so far as unemployment is concerned.

some way in these income tax resolutions_____
perhaps some hidden way, in some obscure language that has not yet been explained to us-there is a provision which would carry out this intention of the government.

Mr. Chairman, there are three main changes in the budget resolution that have to do with reductions in taxation. First of all there is the proposed reduction in the corporation tax. It is proposed that the 21 per cent or lower rate should apply to the first $35,000 instead of the first $25,000. This will mean that a corporation with a net income of $30,000 will save $1,500 or a corporation with a net income of $35,000 or more will save about $3,000. This is hardly enough to put one man to work and it can hardly be considered a stimulus to the economy.
This afternoon I heard the Minister of Labour talk about double depreciation and, after listening to the formula he put forward, it is my opinion that no greater farce has ever been presented to the House of Commons. I can quite understand that the Minister of Finance is not very much interested in unemployment.

On a point of order,
Mr. Chairman, I thought you had already ruled that this subject was out of order.

He has not ruled that we should not touch on this subject. Either we should deal with unemployment or we should not do so, and I can readily see in this announcement the idea of the minister that there is no emergency with respect to unemployment.
The second change in the Income Tax Act is the elimination of the 4 per cent tax imposed on investment income exceeding $2,500. I can quite readily see that this is a measure to entice people to buy government bonds. Government bonds have been very unpopular with investors, and by removing this tax I think the minister will attain his objective of getting more people to buy his heretofore rather unpopular government bonds.

In my opinion the minister might also have included in the resolution a provision by which those people who obtain an honorarium for their work in

I shall, as usual, Mr. Chairman, be brief and strictly in order, the precedent having been set by the hon. member for Welland. First of all, I want to say that I am sure there are numerous small companies that will welcome the first clause in this income tax resolution which provides that the amount of income on which the tax rate of 21 per cent shall apply will be increased from $25,000 to $35,000. I know of a number of small companies, particularly those

operating in the primary industries, that are finding conditions not too easy at the present time. This concession will be welcomed by those companies which will, in some cases, continue to operate under great difficulties and in other cases will try to expand, still under great difficulties.
However, Mr. Chairman, in that connection I may say I have always felt there was a certain academic approach to taxation on the part of ministers of finance and, more particularly, on the part of some of the senior officers. I say that with all respect for their ability and the service they are performing for this country. I understand that the Minister of Finance has had a very distinguished career in the legal profession, but that is very limiting. In some respects, lawyers are excellent people. However, I have found them to be something like preachers in that they are very theoretical. I do suggest it would be a good thing if the minister and some of his senior officials were to visit certain typical small industries in this country because when they are laying out rates of taxation on paper it is often done on the basis of arithmetic and without a great deal of knowledge of the circumstances under which certain of our people operate.
In illustration of this I might say that I know of one small company operating under considerable difficulty with all the risks that are involved in the forestry and lumber industries. There are many that are not seen by the Minister of Finance or on occasion by their senior officials. This company has an investment of close to $100,000 but would realize less profit than a ten by ten stall dispensing coca cola and comic magazines to school children. These different circumstances do exist. I suggest, as I have suggested before, that it would be a good idea, particularly for some of the senior officials, to acquire firsthand knowledge of the circumstances under which certain typical industries in this country operate.
With respect to clause 12 of the income tax resolution, I might say that I was very glad to see the original clause and to know that there has been some amendment widening the basis of this clause. This will be of considerable assistance to those persons with limited financial resources seeking a university education. I would suggest that the minister give consideration to the inclusion of living expenses up to a certain family income limit. I am not suggesting that children of wealthy families should receive this consideration, but certainly those children in families of limited incomes should be given some sort of consideration in this regard. I feel that we should do everything
Income Tax Act
possible to make certain that as many young people as possible obtain university education.
Mr. Chairman, I should like very briefly to refer to the situation in respect to those persons who engage voluntarily in the extinguishing of fires, particularly in small communities. I should like to support the remarks made by the member for Welland in his suggestion that some consideration should be given to those voluntary fire brigade men who receive honorariums for their services as such. Mr. Chairman, in view of your anxiety I shall retreat from this attack.
I want very briefly to mention that the Canadian Medical Association has made representations to the minister with respect to the deduction of expenses for refresher courses. I would urge the minister to give consideration to these representations of the Canadian Medical Association when he is dealing with his main budget later this year.

I should like to address myself to the first few words in this resolution which are:
Resolved that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide among other things:
It will be noted that "other things" which the government is recommending are specified, but it does not tell us what the government is in fact recommending. I think there will be very great disappointment in regard to many of these other things. There are one or two other things which I think ought to be included so that it will be possible for us to pass this resolution with expediency.
Instead of relying upon an order in council made in secret I think that the government should amend the Income Tax Act specifically to carry out the intended policy announced by the Minister of Finance on December 20, which appears at 1007 of Hansard. His statement contained therein is as follows.
I fully share this optimism about the capabilities of Canadian industry. I am anxious to do everything within our means to encourage initiative and enterprise. As a powerful incentive to these ends I am pleased to announce measures to fulfil three major purposes: first, to assist new industries in areas where there is a substantial degree of continued unemployment over the years;
I would argue, sir, that there should be specific provisions put into the act by this

Income Tax Act
parliament at this session to cover that because, as the minister said, it was a major new thing. I contend that a major new thing should be done by parliament and not done, under the colour of some provision already in the Income Tax Act, by order in council. It seems to me that if the minister thought this important enough to include in his budget speech as a new proposal, it should be among the "other things" referred to in the second line of the resolution now before us.
As found at page 1007 of Hansard, the minister goes on to say as follows:
-second, to aid the development of new products from processing operations not hitherto carried on in Canada;
I think there should be a specific provision spelled out so that we in parliament know what this is and have some voice in its condition and some say with regard to how this is to be done instead of its being done in secret by the governor in council. I suggest that this provision should be included in this resolution, and it will not be expedient to pass this resolution, in my opinion, unless that provision is included.
The minister goes on to say:
-third, to encourage the production of new types of goods. Double depreciation will, at the option of the taxpayer be allowed in respect of capital expenditures incurred in the first year for these purposes, but may be applied in any of the first three years.
I would argue, sir, that it may be possible for the governor in council to do that under existing law, but I suggest that when the existing law was made, the use of the law for this purpose was not contemplated. For that reason and because this is new I regard this as something that should be done by parliament and not by order in council.
We have been told something about how one of these three things was going to be accomplished. I am not going to transgress your ruling, sir, by discussing this but I must say that we were not told by the Minister of Labour under what authority, what law, or what statute the policy announced today was being carried out by the governor in council or by the Minister of Labour. We do not know. We are still in ignorance of this.
I would point out again that on December 20 the Minister of Finance produced this as a new policy. I repeat that it is my opinion that parliament should decide the main lines of that policy not in detail but in a broad sense. These details should be decided by parliament and not by the governor in council. Parliament should decide which are the areas of continued unemployment. It is this parliament that is going to relieve certain taxpayers of burdens that other taxpayers will have.

That is something that should be done by parliament here and not by governor in council.
I say that the minister should bring in amendments to this resolution-obviously he cannot argue that this would effect the ways and means because he proposes to do it in any event by order in council-and incorporate them in it so that we as the representatives of the people may have a voice in regard to how these things are done. I would urge the minister to give consideration to the suggestion that the law in respect of these policies be included in this resolution instead of these things being done by order in council or in the cabinet. The law in respect to the policy, to which the government attached so much importance last December, should be dealt with by parliament.

Before this clause as amended is carried would the minister care to express an opinion as to whether or not this clause amounts in its effect to another tax on the municipalities and provinces in connection with their borrowing? Reducing the yield to foreign investors would necessarily increase the cost of borrowing to Canadian municipalities and provinces and therefore increase the burden which presently exists due to the high cost of raising money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My answer to that question is, no. This is not an additional tax on municipalities. It is, however, an increase in the withholding tax as applied to the payment of interest by the municipality to nonresident bond holders in respect of bonds issued after December 20, 1960. I stress the fact that this resolution and the withholding tax thereby proposed have no application whatever to any outstanding obligations of 90205-6-166J
Income Tax Act
municipalities up to the date of the budget. In this respect the proposal differs from one which Mr. Ilsley brought forward some 20 years ago. He put forward a similar proposal and at that time he proposed to apply it to all outstanding issues as well as to future issues. There was no little flurry over that, and the resolution in its original form was withdrawn by Mr. Ilsley.
This will have no effect whatever on issues outstanding at December 20, 1960. With respect to issues after that date I think the hon. member will agree that it is very much better for municipalities to do the raising of funds by their bond issues in Canada rather than abroad. I am sure the hon. member must share the concern which I have felt and expressed in budget speeches in previous years over the raising by some municipalities and some provinces of loans in the New York market. They were losing on account of the premium on the Canadian dollar sometimes as much as 5 per cent of their borrowing, and in addition to that they were facing on the day of maturity the prospect that the exchange rate might have changed and that they might be confronted with a further loss if the Canadian dollar at that time should be not at a premium but at a discount.
The Canadian market has shown since the budget that it is quite capable of absorbing the issues which have been offered to it. I mentioned recently that in the first six weeks of this new calendar year provincial and municipal bond issues to the amount of $200 million and a federal issue in February of $150 million had been fully absorbed in Canada without the slightest disturbance of interest rates. In this period the market tended to strengthen and there was a slight reduction in the prevailing interest rates, subject, of course, to the usual fluctuations.
So I think the answer which might be given to the questions and observations of the hon. member is, in all the circumstances, a reassuring one.

I share the minister's concern about Canadian borrowing in New York. 1 am sure he appreciates the reason why so many municipalities have had to go to New York in the last few years is the chaotic conditions in the Canadian money market which he and his colleagues have created. This has been a source of concern to us all.
I think the minister will also agree on reflection that if these changes which he is now proposing do increase the prices at which municipalities and provinces can borrow money, it is in fact an extra tax or an additional burden which he is placing on the already over-burdened municipalities.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the ruling of the Chair in committee that the announcement made by the Minister of Labour today could not be discussed on the
income tax resolution, I should like to suggest to the leader of the house that he call the estimates of the Department of Labour tomorrow so that this matter can be discussed in view of the great public interest in it and its urgency.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we always give careful consideration to suggestions from the other side but so many people are waiting to discuss another matter of great public interest, namely, agriculture, that I think perhaps we should go on with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture tomorrow as announced earlier this week.

In that case would the leader of the house allow me to make an alternative suggestion, that the government move on Monday to go into committee of supply in order to give the opposition an opportunity-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: You had it last week.

If the minister would not interrupt, it would be appreciated. May I suggest that the government on Monday move to go into committee of supply in order to give the opposition an opportunity to discuss the announcement made today which there was certainly no opportunity to debate before today.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: In view of these suggestions which will be given careful consideration, I will not announce any business other than that for tomorrow.

speechtext:
What Is the result of the investigation referred to by the Minister of Transport in his answer to the question regarding lake Williams, Nova Scotia, as reported in Hansard for Friday, August 5, 1960, at page 7598?
Answer by: Hon. Leon Balcer (Minister of Transport):
Question
A Department of Transport report of the inquiry into the accident to Piper J-3CG5 aircraft, CF-DGT, at lake Williams, Nova Scotia, on May 22, 1960, revealed that the accident occurred because the pilot in command failed to see the sailboat until too late to avoid a collision while he was taxiing his aircraft at high speed into the sun.
Seaplane operations at lake Williams, Nova Scotia, have been thoroughly investigated by officers of the Department of Transport and those operations are, and will be, kept under strict supervision in order to make certain that the air regulations are being observed and that such operations are being conducted in a safe and orderly manner.
